items.title: Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?
items.summary: Ukraine needs another satellite internet service, but a decent alternative to Elon Musk's network doesn't exist - yet.
items.content:
Image caption, A man offers residents in Kherson, Ukraine, the use of his Starlink internet after a Russian strike
Ukraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet.
Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network.
That vulnerability was highlighted by Musk himself on Saturday, when he accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by using it for "drone strikes to kill people".
Saying that loophole was closed last week, he wrote on X , external : "Violation of those terms will result in end of service."
He added: "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately".
There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation.
France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared with Starlink's 10,000-plus.
The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, IrisÂ², however it won't be up and running until 2029.
For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death.
"God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line."
For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones.
Figure caption, Watch: Who controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?
Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years.
Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield, which is controlled by the US government, for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks.
"You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations.
Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored , highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate.
"Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted.
Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Musk.
While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS.
"This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control."
Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/ Getty Images
Image caption, Ukrainian soldiers set up a Starlink terminal on the battlefield
Starlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to agree.
Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield", a soldier said.
The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone.
Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones", said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company.
They are also about five times more expensive, she added.
Rhetoric from the White House - like Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC.
She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon.
Comments from Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted , external at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable.
Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently", a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC.
Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom.
But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for.
That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs.
Image caption, French President Emmanuel Macron, with a Eutelsat terminal, at the International Paris Air Show last year
Eva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing because, as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive.
Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve".
No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield.
But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage."
Govsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, IrisÂ² , external is up and running in 2029.
The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared ) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one.
Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE.
It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen.
"Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that IrisÂ² is planning for less satellites."
Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid".
Image caption, A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying 56 Starlink satellites takes off from Cape Canaveral in March 2023
A highly produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With IrisÂ², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity."
So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea.
"Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity."
It's similar to how mobile phones work, explained Eva Berneke: "If you don't have 5G, you go back to 4G. And if you don't have 4G, you might use 3G, so you have multiple networks for resilience. It's the same idea in warfare."
But while a phone might not load pictures as quickly on 3G, for a drone operator, it can be deadly: "That is not a nice situation to have to be in when you're fighting a war."
IrisÂ² is not the only option. This week, Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE , external announced they would look at developing satellite communications for Ukraine's military defences.
And a joint venture between European satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, called Project Bromo, is hoped to be another competitor against SpaceX, but it is still in the very early phases.
Space projects take a long time, Berneke said, and need " a lot of money".
Designing the programme, making the satellites, launching them and then having enough of them in orbit for full coverage takes many years.
"Even if you gave me â¬8bn right now, I don't think I could have anything up there before 2032-2033," she explained.
Military work in Space is nothing new, and has been happening since the dawn of the space age in the 1950s. But the conflict in Ukraine has shown how integral it is to modern warfare.
"Communication is so important, and terrestrial communication platforms, whether it's 5G or fibre, can be attacked on the ground," Berneke said. "It is a lot harder to shoot down an entire satellite network. That's not something any military can do right now."
While we look to the skies, however, most of the world's communications are travelling via undersea cables - about 99% in fact. But these are vulnerable to attack - this week the UK government outlined new measures to protect its cables, after an increase in suspicious activity by Russian vessels.
"In a crisis or conflict, there are serious concerns that undersea cables will be cut... so if that happens it's good to have satellite communication as a backup," Kari Bingen said.

items.title: Prediction: A Stock Market Crash Is Coming. Here's What Investors Should Do Based on Warren Buffett's Advice. - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Prediction: A Stock Market Crash Is Coming. Here's What Investors Should Do Based on Warren Buffett's Advice.  The Motley Fool
items.content:
Stocks generally trend higher over the long term, but it's getting harder to ignore the growing chorus of risks that could derail the current bull market. Neocloud companies, which operate artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, are finding it harder to access affordable funding to build more infrastructure, which could put a dent in the sales of semiconductor suppliers like Nvidia .
Moreover, rising oil prices are stoking inflation, which prompted the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its September meeting, and more hikes might be on the horizon. High interest rates can be a major headwind for the stock market, particularly now, when so many tech companies are borrowing money to build AI infrastructure.
To make matters worse, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.52% ) is trading at the second-highest valuation in its history, behind only the peak of the dot-com internet bubble in the year 2000. In my view, this leaves the index especially vulnerable to a crash, but legendary investor Warren Buffett has some excellent advice for navigating these very situations.
A series of global geopolitical challenges are roiling the energy markets right now. The U.S. and Iran have been locked in a conflict since late February, resulting in the closure of the Strait of Hormuz waterway, through which 25% of the world's seaborne oil normally transits each day. The ongoing war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen also took a turn for the worse recently, while Ukraine and Russia continue to target one another's energy infrastructure, knocking even more supply offline.
As a result, the price of a single barrel of West Texas Intermediate crude oil has surged by 72% this year to $98, driving up the cost of gasoline, diesel, and even jet fuel. That means consumers are paying more for every product that travels by truck, boat, or plane, which includes groceries, retail goods, and more.
This is stoking inflation in a very big way. In fact, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose at an annualized rate of 3.7% in September, substantially higher than the Federal Reserve's 2% target. The Fed raised the federal funds rate (overnight interest rates) by 25 basis points at its September meeting to put the brakes on the economy and cool prices down, and chairman Kevin Warsh warned there might be more hikes to come.
Rising interest rates could derail this bull market
The Fed's last rate-hiking cycle spanned from March 2022 to August 2023, when policymakers were trying to tame the previous surge in inflation. The S&P 500 suffered a bear market decline of 20% during that period, and history could repeat.
Rising interest rates are bad for stocks for a few reasons. First, they force consumers to allocate more of their household income to debt repayments, leaving less room for discretionary spending. Second, high rates make companies think twice about borrowing money to fund their expansion plans, limiting their growth potential. These two factors hurt corporate earnings, and earnings drive stock prices over the long term.
Third, rising interest rates increase the yield on risk-free assets like cash and government Treasury bonds , giving investors an alternative to stocks. These assets are very popular during periods of uncertainty, because they give investors a guaranteed return.
The S&P 500 is trading at a Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio of 40.9 as I write this (Oct. 22), a shade below its all-time high of 44.2 from the peak of the dot-com bubble in 2000. Personally, I don't think seasoned investors will be lining up to pay a premium for stocks in this environment, and some might even use this as a chance to cash in their gains from the last few years. As a result, the perfect storm might be brewing.
Warren Buffett served as the CEO of the Berkshire Hathaway holding company from 1965 to 2025. Had you invested just $500 in Berkshire stock when he took the helm and never sold, it would have been worth a whopping $24 million by the time he stepped down. The same investment in the S&P 500 would have grown to just $199,851 over the same period, so Buffett had a knack for picking winning stocks.
In his 1986 letter to Berkshire's shareholders, Buffett said, "We simply attempt to be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy only when others are fearful." Simply put, he would buy stocks aggressively during downturns in the broader market, because he knew the upward trend would always prevail over the long term.
Buffett also consistently reminded investors that stocks aren't just financial instruments that move up and down -- they represent real businesses with real fundamentals. A person wouldn't sell their house on a whim just because its value dropped during a given year, so selling a stock for the same reason makes very little sense. As long as the underlying business is healthy, a decline in stock price should be used as an opportunity to buy more.
As a result, while stock market turbulence can be unnerving, investors might want to get ready to put some money to work.

Alphabet Inc. (GOOG, GOOGL) could be positioning its artificial intelligence chips as a serious challenge to Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), with third-party Tensor Processing Unit sales potentially becoming a major new revenue stream, according to IO Fund analyst Beth Kindig.
In a note on Friday, Kindig said Google's advantage may not come from simply building a faster accelerator, but from attacking the economics of AI infrastructure, particularly the cost of running increasingly expensive AI workloads.
Read Next TeraWulf CEO Paul Prager Turns Elon Musk’s ‘Stranded Compute’ Warning Into A Buying Pitch Anushka Basu
She said Google’s AI story is about to change “not from advancements in AI software, but by going after one of the most profitable hardware businesses the tech industry has ever seen.”
Alphabet’s Class A shares closed 1% lower in Friday’s regular trading session, while  Nvidia shares fell about 0.6%.
Kindig Points To Google Targeting AI's Biggest Cost Problem With TPU Strategy
Kindig says the AI accelerator market is entering a new phase as Google moves its merchant TPU strategy from announcement toward commercial execution. Google recognized its first TPU-related revenue from third-party customers in the second quarter.
The analyst noted that the focus is increasingly on cost per token now, as massive AI infrastructure spending puts pressure on Big Tech's free cash flow.
Google's latest TPU 8t and 8i systems are designed to improve performance per dollar compared with the previous-generation Ironwood TPU. Kindig says TPU 8i can deliver up to an 80% improvement in performance per dollar, particularly for low-latency inference workloads, while TPU 8t offers up to 2.7 times better performance per dollar for training.
The result could allow customers to process substantially more AI workloads for the same infrastructure spending.
“Google’s greatest competitive advantage may not be building a faster chip than Nvidia, but rather in building AI infrastructure at a lower cost,” she added.
Kindig believes that the bigger opportunity for Google could come from the company selling TPUs directly to third-party customers rather than exclusively deploying them through Google Cloud.
She added that this would create a second revenue stream for Google while shifting much of the upfront infrastructure burden toward customers, including data centers, power, cooling and hardware.
Anthropic is already expected to deploy a gigawatt of Ironwood TPUs in 2026, followed by 5GW of TPU 8i in 2027 and another 10GW in 2028, according to Broadcom's update cited by Kindig, who believes that this would create a significant revenue stream for the company.
At the high end, that would represent a staggering acceleration for Google's chip business, potentially reaching the current run rate of its Search business in just a few years, the analyst noted.
Google Could Challenge Nvidia Beyond Inference, Says Kindig
Google's threat to Nvidia also extends beyond inference. Kindig highlights TPU 8t's ability to scale to a 9,600-chip superpod with 2PB of shared HBM and 121 exaflops of FP4 compute.
Google's Virgo Network fabric can then connect 14 such superpods, creating a domain capable of supporting 134,400 TPUs.
The scale could become particularly important if Nvidia encounters further delays with its next-generation systems, potentially giving Google additional room to gain accelerator share, she added.
Retail sentiment on Stocktwits around Alphabet trended in the ‘bullish’ territory at the time of writing.
GOOGL stock is up 2% year-to-date, while  NVDA stock is up 13%. The Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) is up 15% over the past 12 months, while the iShares U.S. Technology ETF (IYW) is up 25%.

items.title: More than 1,300 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
items.summary: Hundreds of thousands took part in demonstrations in France, with protests also taking place in other European countries.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protesters during skirmishes
More than 1,300 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France on Saturday that were followed by some clashes later in the day, officials have said.
After largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.
Officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.
The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.
Katya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them
Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.
The interior ministry said 53 officers were hurt in clashes across the country on Saturday.
French President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings.
Image caption, In the southern port of Marseille, protesters erected makeshift street barricades and set them alight late on Saturday
Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.
Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.
French Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", news agency AFP reported.
The Interior Ministry said 142 people were arrested in the French capital on Saturday, less than half of the number arrested on the same day last week.
Image caption, Protesters clash with police at a demonstration in Bordeaux
In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.
Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.
In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture.
"There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.
NuÃ±ez also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France. He said the number of arrests across the country would likely rise.
The man in Toulouse, a 20-year-old protester, had several fingers torn off one hand when a nearby explosive went off, Franceinfo reported, citing the medic who treated him.
As the unrest continued into the early hours of Sunday morning, authorities in Bouches-du-RhÃ´ne, the region in which Marseilles sits, said seven businesses had been "looted or damaged".
Image caption, "We really want a change in France," a teenage protester told the BBC
Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office.
"They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.
Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government.
"I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."
He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".
Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally (RN) party in the north-central city of OrlÃ©ans, which proceeded peacefully.
The recent unrest has played out against a backdrop of a polarised political landscape, with France preparing for what could be the most divisive election period in a generation.
Macron will leave office next spring and polls suggest French voters will ultimately face a choice between RN's candidate Marine Le Pen and that of the radical-left La France Insoumise (France Unbowed).
Leading figures from both parties have levelled the blame for the disorder at Macron, though right-wing figures have also heaped criticism on rioters while left-wing leaders support the union-led protests.
LFI candidate Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon said French media had not covered the peaceful protests while police had created "a setup deliberately designed to provoke chaos" that had "mutilated two people".
Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.
In Barcelona, more than 120 people were arrested after a student protest descended into what local authorities described as "gratuitous violence".
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.
In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.
Image caption, People clash with police during a demonstration against the high cost of living in Bordeaux.
Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.
Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to AFP, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.
The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.
The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers.

President Donald Trump Just Proclaimed, "Tariffs Don't Cause Inflation, They Cause Wealth," but Data From Federal Reserve Economists Show Otherwise
From a purely statistical standpoint, Wall Street has enjoyed having President Donald Trump in the White House. Even accounting for a few periods of historic volatility (e.g., the COVID-19 crash in February-March 2020 and the tariff tantrum of April 2025), the average annual return of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI), S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) has been higher under Trump than under most presidents since the late 1890s.
However, this doesn't mean that all of the president's policies are necessarily well-received on Wall Street. For example, Trumpflation (inflation specifically driven by Donald Trump's policies) is a genuine threat to the artificial intelligence (AI)-driven bull market.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
President Trump's tariffs are doing more harm than good. Image source: Official White House Photo by Daniel Torok.
President Trump sees things differently. While speaking to an audience at a campaign rally in Montana ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Trump touched on inflation and the role his tariff and trade policy may have played in it. Said the president:
We don't have inflation, and tariffs don't cause inflation. You know what they cause? Wealth.
Although Trump insists that tariffs aren't contributing to persistently elevated inflation and are beneficial to the U.S. economy, reports from New York Federal Reserve economists show otherwise .
Tariffs have been foundational to Donald Trump's presidency
While tariffs have been a hot-button topic since Trump's second non-consecutive term began in January 2025, they've been a theme throughout both of his terms. In 2018, the Trump administration kicked off a trade war with China, imposing tariffs on washing machines, solar panels, steel, aluminum, and various tech goods.
To encourage overseas companies to manufacture their U.S.-bound products in America
To make U.S. products more price-competitive with those being imported
Shortly after the start of his second term, he introduced a new round of tariffs. Trump's April 2025 "Liberation Day" tariffs imposed a sweeping global duty and higher reciprocal tariffs on dozens of countries deemed to have adverse trade imbalances with America. A majority of these tariffs, imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, were invalidated by the U.S. Supreme Court in February 2026.
In late July, the Trump administration imposed new sweeping global duties, ranging from 10% to 12.5%, on more than 80 countries under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. These new tariffs cover more than 99% of U.S. imports.
While President Trump has frequently praised tariffs for bringing in extra revenue, New York Federal Reserve economists have found that the president's tariffs are doing more harm than good.
Donald Trump's tariffs are raising consumer prices, according to Federal Reserve economists
Recently, three NY Federal Reserve economists writing for Liberty Street Economics dug into the impact of President Trump's 2025 tariffs on consumer prices. In "How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through into Consumer Prices," the trio of authors found clear evidence that tariffs cause inflation.
According to the report, every percentage point increase in average tariffs equated to a quarter-percentage-point increase in consumer goods prices after one year. Economists estimate that Trump's tariffs have added 2.9 percentage points to goods price inflation by February 2026. Here's the kicker: economists estimate that goods prices would have modestly declined without the president's tariffs.
The authors homed in on three catalysts that have lifted consumer prices:
Tariffs directly raise prices for imported goods, with overseas companies rarely absorbing tariff costs.
Higher input costs. Adding duties to unfinished imported goods (e.g., steel) used to complete the manufacture of a product domestically can increase production costs, which are then passed on to consumers.
In some instances where tariffs made imported goods notably pricier than U.S.-made products, domestic manufacturers would increase their prices to capture some of this difference.
A separate Liberty Street Economics report from December 2024 ("Do Import Tariffs Protect U.S. Firms?") also uncovered negative correlations from Donald Trump's 2018 China tariffs.
The four economists who contributed to this report highlighted the effects of input tariffs in raising consumer prices. Perhaps more importantly, the authors found a clear correlation between public companies whose stock declined on China tariff announcement days and worse future real outcomes.
The public companies that performed poorly on tariff announcement days were associated with declines in employment, labor productivity, sales, and profits from 2019-2021. In other words, the adverse effects of Trump's tariffs endured for years after they were enacted.
President Trump's tariffs are one of the two policies directly lifting consumer prices at the moment. The Trump-led Iran war is the other catalyst. The ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz has led to the largest energy supply disruption in modern times, sending gas and diesel prices soaring.
Federal Reserve policymakers have been left with little choice but to undertake only the fourth interest rate-hiking cycle of the 21st century. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and 11 other members of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted unanimously to raise the federal funds target rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00% on Sept. 16.
However, the FOMC's battle against persistently elevated inflation is far from over. Sticky core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, coupled with near-record-high diesel prices, will likely prompt several additional rate hikes over the next year.
Historically, Fed rate-hiking cycles have coincided with strong economic growth and healthy bull markets. But this time may very well be different.
The stock market entered 2026 at its second-priciest valuation in history and can ill afford any speed bumps or potholes. If the FOMC gets aggressive with rate hikes to deliver price stability, the AI-driven stock market could pay the price. Even a relatively small slowdown in the AI data center build-out or AI growth projections due to higher interest rates may be enough to send the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite over the edge.

An election billboard of President Iliana Iotova and vice presidential candidate Kiril Valchev in Sofia, Bulgaria, on October 23, 2026 [Nikolay Doychinov/AFP]
Polls have opened in Bulgaria’s presidential election after a campaign that focused on growing economic hardship and drone attacks on Black Sea shipping.
Before Sunday’s vote, President Iliana Iotova, 61, and former caretaker Prime ⁠Minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, were leading a field of 27 candidates in the polls.

list 2 of 3 Bulgaria searches for missing crew after drones hit two ships in Black Sea
list 3 of 3 Bulgaria ends search for missing crew after drone strike sinks cargo ship
⁠The presidency is a largely ceremonial post in Bulgaria. While major policies must be approved by parliament, direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, sign international treaties and appoint ambassadors.
The election has also gained attention after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria that likely killed about two dozen international seafarers.
The drone strikes ‌sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of Russia’s war on Ukraine, prompting Bulgaria to seek help from its allies to bolster its maritime security.
The Bulgarian government has stopped short of explicitly blaming Russia for the attacks, but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the outcome of the strikes “benefits the Russian Federation”.
The two leading candidates for president have both condemned the strikes, but they differ on the broader war in Ukraine.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is backed by ⁠pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He ⁠signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
“I want Bulgaria to have a voice of its own in Europe, a reliable NATO ally that defends its interests through preparedness, strong diplomacy and ⁠a clear position,” he said at a rally on Thursday.
A rescue operation is carried out at the ship Chelsea 3 near Byala, Bulgaria, on October 13, 2026, after it was hit by drones [Handout/Bulgarian Ministry of Interior via AP] Iotova, a former vice president, became acting president in January after Radev resigned to ⁠enter the parliamentary race, which he won on what many ⁠political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket.
Radev supports Iotova, and they both have called for a diplomatic end to the war.
“My opponents argue that there must be ‌a war of attrition,” Iotova said at a rally on Thursday. “The truth is, we are all the ones who are most exhausted.”
While there is a broad consensus among the parties in parliament on the country’s pro-Western path, widespread pro-Russian sentiments based on traditional historical and cultural ties with Russia have divided society, particularly since the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Dobromir Zhivkov, managing director of the Market Links polling agency, said Iotova is among those who advocate that Bulgaria should take a more neutral position.
“They call for an end to aid for Ukraine and a halt to arms deliveries to Ukraine. We often hear them use Kremlin rhetoric and terminology borrowed directly from Kremlin propaganda,” he told The Associated Press news agency this past week.
Candidates are also addressing public fears about the steep rise in energy prices and surging inflation as many Bulgarians in rural areas struggle to make ends meet.
Polls by Alpha Research suggested Iotova would win 41 percent of the vote and ‌Gyurov ‌28 percent.
Voting started at 7am (05:00 GMT), and polls close at 8pm (18:00 GMT).
Analysts expected none of the 27 candidates to secure the outright majority needed to win in the first round, however.
Turnout must also be above 50 percent of the 6.6 million registered voters, and Sunday’s turnout is expected to be less than 40 percent, which means a likely run-off on November 1.

Protesters fly a French flag amid clashes in Paris on Saturday [Reuters/Abdul Saboor]
Several Western European nations have expressed their opposition to the potential resumption of the Iran war, as spiralling global oil prices have worsened the cost of living crisis across Europe.
Countries such as Germany and the UK, among other major powers, which initially remained silent on the US-Israeli bombardment of Iran, have aired their views, calling for diplomacy to end the war which has disrupted global oil supplies.

Continued disruption to energy supplies is pushing up household costs as winter in Europe approaches, adding fuel to protests over living standards that have engulfed European capitals in recent weeks.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei on Sunday drew attention to what he described as a shift in Germany’s position on attacks against Iran.
In a post on X, Baghaei recalled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s remarks during Israel’s June 2025 military campaign: “This is the dirty work Israel is doing for all of us.”
He contrasted those words with German officials’ recent warnings against renewed attacks and calls to prevent further escalation, before citing Friedrich Schiller’s The Maid of Orleans, quoting a passage that portrays reason being helplessly dragged towards an abyss by the forces of madness.
Experts say Baghaei’s remarks reflect a broader shift across Europe, where leaders are increasingly questioning their support for the US-Israeli war on Iran.
With Washington reportedly preparing options for renewed attacks, what would further escalation mean for Europe and could the war further strain already frayed relations with the United States?
When the US and Israel launched their attacks on February 28 , the leaders of Britain, France and Germany issued a joint statement condemning Iran’s retaliatory strikes on countries across the region. “We condemn Iranian attacks on countries in the region in the strongest terms,” British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, French President Emmanuel Macron and Merz said.
Their statement did not condemn the opening US-Israeli attacks. However, it called for negotiations to follow. Nearly eight months into the war, European governments are now explicitly warning against another military campaign.
On Friday, the foreign ministers of Britain, France, Germany and Italy met their counterparts from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt in Istanbul to discuss the conflict and the Strait of Hormuz. Further escalation between Iran and the US “would create nothing but losers and would undoubtedly have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.
“And so the first thing this group of eight countries … will do is call on both sides to exercise the utmost restraint, because we cannot afford another escalation in the region,” he added.
The warnings against new attacks do not necessarily mean European governments have abandoned their positions on Iran’s nuclear programme or regional activities, but they do show a change of position and have revealed that European governments are not united in their approach to the Iran war.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has consistently opposed the US-Israeli campaign. At this month’s European summit, he again described the war as “illegal, unjust and unjustified”, linking it to Europe’s mounting economic costs.
Western countries have opposed Iran’s nuclear programme, which Tehran says is for civilian purposes only. European countries were part of the landmark 2015 nuclear deal with Iran that limited Tehran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief. But during his first term in 2018, United States President Donald Trump withdrew from the deal. Both the US and Israel invoked Iran’s nuclear programme to launch their attack in February.
Europe’s divisions have been particularly visible over access to military bases and airspace. “We did not participate in these strikes, but are in close contact with our international partners, including the United States, Israel and partners in the region,” said the February 28 statement from Britain, France and Germany.
But non-participation in the opening attacks did not mean European countries would uniformly refuse support for subsequent operations. Germany said early in the war that it would not restrict US use of its bases, including Ramstein, a major American military hub.
Britain initially withheld permission for the opening attacks. However, it authorised US use of British bases for what London described as specific, limited defensive strikes against Iranian facilities involved in attacks on regional allies. Then, after initial reluctance, Britain expanded that permission to include operations against missile sites and capabilities being used to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
France allowed US support aircraft at Istres, while saying they would support the defence of regional partners rather than participate in attacks on Iran. It later blocked a weapons flight to Israel connected to the campaign. Spain went further. After refusing permission for attacks from the jointly operated Rota and Moron bases, Madrid closed its airspace to US aircraft involved in the war.
Those were different restrictions with different purposes, rather than a single European refusal to cooperate, but they provoked Trump. Calling Spain “terrible”, he threatened to cut off trade and said Washington wanted “nothing to do with Spain”.
The dispute has therefore exposed a widening argument over whether alliance commitments require European governments to facilitate a war they did not choose.
Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera: “As to whether the war might push European leaders to openly challenge Trump, and limit support, it is certainly possible. What was initially a diplomatic disagreement is turning into something that has much more direct … and we could see increased resistance to any support from European countries.”
After Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening strikes, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said there was “renewed hope for the people of Iran”. She also warned then that instability could push the region into a spiral of violence. But by October 16, the costs to Europe had become central to her message. “Households and industry are paying the price for a war far beyond our borders,” she said after an EU summit.
According to von der Leyen, Europe’s bill for imported fossil fuels had increased by 106 billion euros, while gas prices had risen about 140 percent since late February and diesel prices had doubled.
Disruption to Gulf supplies and restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have also caused energy prices to spike. Brent crude settled at $72.48 a barrel on February 27, before the war began. It reached $126.41 at the end of April and remains well above $100 a barrel, with no sign of falling any time soon.
“For Europe, there is the economic interest as well, knowing it would further take a toll on energy markets, pushing up prices at a time when European countries are going into winter and the pushback to that,” Julie Norman, an associate fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera.
Hilborne added that “there is an impact as well on food and fertiliser … The Persian Gulf is a hub for nitrogen-based fertilisers and disruptions have sent prices of urea up by something like 70 percent. Also, supply chains are feeling the impact as well, as shipping companies are facing large increases in their insurance premiums and/or need to reroute to longer journeys”.
“I would say that the Iranian war has had a direct, measurable and quite a rapid impact on European prices,” he added.
The search for relief from the energy crisis has created further friction, with Washington pressing European governments to release emergency diesel stocks, while Trump eased restrictions on Russian diesel in an effort to lower prices. That move provoked criticism from Ukraine and its supporters, who warned that renewed energy revenues would strengthen Moscow’s war effort.
But some of the sharpest political consequences are unfolding closer to home. Protests over living costs, housing, wages and public services have been seen across France, Belgium, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Greece and Albania. Their causes vary, and they do not constitute a single coordinated movement, but experts say the cost of living crisis, compounded by price rises caused by the Iran war, is a common thread that unites the protesters across the continent.
Donatella della Porta, a sociologist and political scientist, told Al Jazeera that opposition to war was central to recent protests by young people across Europe, alongside anger over military spending at the expense of welfare.
She pointed to opposition to military recruitment in schools, weapons-related university research and the use of ports to transport arms, linking those concerns to wider fears about the future.
“Especially the young protesters are afraid that their future will be stolen not only by global warming but also by wars in which they will be sent to die on the battlefield,” she said.
“Young people also connect wars with genocide, having often been socialised into politics during the large protests against the Israeli genocide of the Palestinians.”

A Ukrainian attack led to water and power cuts in occupied Crimea on Saturday, as a barrage of drones in several regions inside Russia left several dead, according to Russian authorities. Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-installed head of the Crimean peninsula, wrote on Telegram that due to the drone attack on local power grids “restrictions on the supply of electricity and water have been put in place”. He did not specify how many households had been affected in Crimea, which is home to more than 2.5 million people. The peninsula, which was seized from Ukraine by Russia in 2014, is a regular target for Ukrainian attacks.
A separate Ukrainian strike in part of the north-eastern Kharkiv region held by Russia killed at least three people and gravely wounded another on Saturday, the Moscow-backed authorities said.
Drones also rained down inside Russia . The country’s defence ministry said 616 of them had been shot down overnight across more than 20 regions of the country. During the day, drones hit Russia’s south-western Bryansk border region, killing at least three people, regional acting governor Yegor Kovalchuc said on Telegram.
In Ukraine, authorities said that at least five people died in several Russian drone and missile strikes in the country’s east. Dnipropetrovsk regional governor Oleksandr Ganzha on Saturday evening said three people were killed and at least 12 wounded when a Russian drone strike hit the town of Synelnykove, setting the fourth floor of a high-rise building on fire. Thousands of British and French troops have taken part in a military training exercise that included one of Britain’s largest airborne operations in two decades, the UK government said on Sunday. The war game is designed to show how Nato countries could be defended against a modern-day attack and comes during fears about Russian aggression in Europe amid Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
About 2,500 troops were involved in the seven-week exercise, in which 600 British and French paratroopers dropped from four RAF A400M Atlas transport aircraft over Germany. The exercise called Rhino Titan, held at the Sennelager military training centre in Germany, has been testing British troops’ ability against an enemy equipped with drones and electronic warfare. “The threats we face in the 21st century require an updated, modern approach to warfare – and our adaptable armed forces are preparing accordingly,” British defence minister Wes Streeting said in a statement.

items.title: From Russian cages to Irish sanctuary: The five-year rescue journey of Bu and Tyapa
items.summary: For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year journey from Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward.
items.content:
Image caption, Tyapa (left) and Bu (right) were previously kept in small cages in the Republic of Dagestan in Russia
After years in cramped cages, two brown bears are adjusting to their new life following a remarkable rescue mission that spanned multiple countries, was disrupted by two major conflicts and involved more than 100 people.
For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year rescue journey from the Republic of Dagestan in Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward.
One bear had spent their life forced to perform in a circus, while the other was confined to a cage so small they could not stand upright.
Today, the bears are now adjusting to a totally different world among the trees and grass at Wild Ireland, a sanctuary for rescued animals in County Donegal.
Image caption, Tyapa is slowly settling into her new surroundings in Burnfoot, County Donegal
Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin first learned about Bu and Tyapa in 2021 and committed to bringing them to safety in Donegal.
The sanctuary, located in Burnfoot, opened in October 2019 and provides a safe space for animals, including brown bears, monkeys, wolves, and lynx.
Image caption, Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin says the bears' health improvements since their arrival have been remarkable
McLaughlin said the two bears were in extremely poor health when they were first rescued.
Former circus bear Bu had spent years confined to a small indoor cage after being forced to perform.
McLaughlin said Tyapa had lived in a cage measuring just 2.5m by 2.5m by 2m, which was too low for him to stand upright and had no roof, which left him exposed to the harsh winters and blistering summer heat.
The bear had no water dish and relied on a hose for drinking water. McLaughlin said he was being raised to be killed for an eventual taxidermy display.
When the bears were rescued, both were severely malnourished and showed signs of psychological trauma.
Blood tests also revealed serious kidney problems associated with prolonged dehydration.
Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 made the original transport route through Ukraine impossible, said McLaughlin.
An alternative route through the Middle East was then explored, but plans were disrupted again in February 2026 when the escalating conflict involving Iran led to airspace closures and flight disruptions across the region.
More than 100 people were involved in the rescue operation, including volunteers, lawyers, veterinarians, animal transport specialists, cargo teams and officials in Russia, the United Arab Emirates and Ireland.
Image caption, The bears travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in the Republic of Ireland on 3 August 2026
In late October 2025, Dima and Yana Kim, who work at Tiger House, a sanctuary near St Petersburg that cares for former circus tigers, embarked on a 36-hour drive to Dagestan to rescue the bears.
Bu and Tyapa had to be cut out of their rusting steel cages, sedated and placed in secure transport crates for the journey back to Tiger House, where they received veterinary treatment and underwent quarantine.
After months of preparation and repeated delays, the bears eventually travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in Ireland in August.
Since arriving at Wild Ireland, McLaughlin said both bears have gained weight, their coats have improved, and follow-up blood tests have shown that their kidney function has returned to normal.
He said their habitat provides woodland, water and room to explore, as well as sheltered areas where they can retreat or move out of public view if they would like some privacy.
"These bears have suffered trauma and the first step of that recovery process is get them back out into the forest, get their paws into the soil and on the grass and get them exploring.
Working with bears is certainly not your everyday job, but for Wild Ireland team member Chloe McElhatton, it's one she absolutely relishes.
Chloe has been working at Wild Ireland for just over a year. She studied zoology at Queen's University Belfast, completing a four-year degree before joining the team.
"This is obviously a very unique job, and it's quite different from what most people would do," she said.
Image caption, Chloe McElhatton is part of the bear team at Wild Ireland and says looking after bears is not your average 9-5 job
"We've done a lot of work hiding food around the bear habitats, encouraging them to search and forage for it themselves and this promotes their natural behaviours and helps them become more comfortable in that new open space," she said.
"Over time, we've seen their confidence build, and you can see great changes, both physically and mentally, in both of them."
Image caption, Liam, who is from France, says the two bears are big and impressive
Liam, who is from France, said the bears were one of his favourite animals to see when visiting the park.
"Very big and very impressive," is how he summed up Bu and Tyapa.
"I saw chickens, some wolves and some monkeys and then the bears which were definitely my favourite."
Image caption, Chris Roberts is a regular visitor to Wild Ireland and came to visit hoping to see a glimpse of the two new bears
Chris Roberts is from Manorcunningham, about 20 minutes from Wild Ireland, and has been visiting the site ever since it first opened in 2019.
"I've lost count of how many times we've been here, but we really wanted to come down today to see if we could catch a glimpse of Bu and Tyapa.
"We absolutely loved it and are delighted to see them doing so well, especially considering their backstory and the awful conditions they were once kept in."

Hormuz Negotiations Between Iran and US Stall as Oil Remains Above $116
Iran's latest attempt to reopen the Strait of Hormuz has become entangled in contradictory messages from Tehran, leaving oil markets facing another week of uncertainty after Brent crude closed Friday above US$116 a barrel.
Iranian ambassador to Pakistan Reza Amiri Moghadam said Saturday that Tehran had offered to restore shipping through the vital waterway if Washington ended its naval blockade of Iranian ports. He accused President Donald Trump of rejecting the proposal.
But Iran's Tasnim news agency subsequently denied that a new offer had been delivered through Pakistani intermediaries.
The conflicting accounts do not establish whether a fresh negotiating initiative exists. They do show that the central dispute remains unresolved: Iran wants relief from the American blockade, while Washington wants navigation through Hormuz restored and concessions on Tehran's nuclear program.
Brent settled Friday at US$116.72 a barrel, according to market reporting, as traders weighed renewed threats against Gulf energy infrastructure and the possibility of further American military action.
Before the war, approximately one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption moved through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global oil chokepoint . The route is also crucial for liquefied natural gas exports, particularly from Qatar. Pipeline bypasses can move some crude, but cannot replicate the strait's full capacity.
In a recent Energi Media interview about Iran and the US midterms , University of Toronto historian Jack Cunningham warned that alternate export routes are not a simple solution: “The problem is a less efficient route is a more costly route.” He also cautioned that Iranian-aligned attacks on infrastructure can threaten routes intended to bypass the strait.
That distinction helps explain why crude prices can remain elevated even when exporters restore some shipments. Transport costs, insurance, the threat of renewed attacks and uncertainty about future supply all influence what buyers pay.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said earlier this month that Tehran's seven-day reopening proposal remained available. The conditions include lifting the US naval blockade and restrictions on Iranian oil exports, alongside a wider cessation of hostilities.
Reuters previously reported that negotiators had explored a phased agreement, but neither side wanted to surrender its principal bargaining chip first. Sunday's competing accounts underscore the difficulty of turning diplomatic signals into an enforceable deal.
The confrontation also has a political deadline: American midterm elections are scheduled for November 3. Cunningham has warned that the conflict increasingly resembles a prolonged war . Higher fuel prices are already adding to household costs, while regional governments face damage to trade and investment.
For Canada, higher crude prices may support revenue for some oil producers while increasing gasoline, diesel, freight and other costs for consumers and businesses. Energi Media has examined how households bear higher energy costs while some producers benefit . The consequences are not uniform, and higher global prices do not guarantee higher profits for every producer.
The LNG implications for British Columbia are equally complicated. Restricted Qatari exports can improve the near-term outlook for competing suppliers, including British Columbia, but long-term investments still depend on future Asian demand and the recovery of Gulf infrastructure.
A diplomatic announcement alone will not restore normal energy trade. Shippers need a credible security arrangement, functioning infrastructure and confidence that neither side will reverse course.
Until those conditions exist, Hormuz will continue to impose costs well beyond the Middle East.

Fireworks and tear gas as protesters and riot police clash in Paris
Fireworks and tear gas as protesters and riot police clash in Paris Close
Police have clashed with protesters in Paris as some demonstrations in France turned violent on Saturday.
A largely peaceful day of protests turned into unrest after nightfall, as protesters were seen throwing objects and fireworks at police.
Around 70,000 officers were deployed across France for a second consecutive weekend and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds.
The Interior Ministry estimated around 400,000 people took part in Saturday's demonstrations, with nearly 1,000 arrests made.
Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from Paris, where he says there are few signs the unrest will ease soon.

items.content:
After the Federal Reserve recently decided to raise interest rates to cool an uptick in inflation, much of Wall Street and Main Street are trying to understand what its next move will be.
According to a recent CNBC article, the chances of a rate hike at the next Federal Reserve meeting in October have fallen below 20%, thanks to a weaker-than-expected September jobs report. However, this doesn’t mean the Federal Reserve won’t continue raising rates at future meetings if the economic environment changes.

Since several economists still believe additional rate hikes are possible, now is the time to start preparing your portfolio to take advantage. Here are a few investments to consider .
Floating-rate CLOs hold a number of corporate loans with floating-rate coupons. When the Fed Funds rate increases, these coupons are usually reset higher.
“The monthly coupons of these ETFs are generated by collateralized loan obligations whose interest is the sum of the SOFR (Secured Overnight Financing Rate) plus a margin,” said Ulrich Ebensperger, founder and CEO of Ziggma . “SOFR is roughly equal to the Fed Funds target rate give or take a few basis points. So not only do the monthly coupons rise with the Fed Rate increase, principal is also protected because of the floating rate nature of the bonds.”
Ebensperger recommended both JAAA and JBBB. JAAA will have lower credit risk because it offers AAA-rated CLO exposure. That lower risk will provide access to a 4.63% 30-day SEC yield. JBBB offers investors a higher 30-day SEC yield of 6.34%, but that comes with greater default risk . No matter the risk you want to take, these products will see higher yields if the Fed raises rates again.
Senior loan ETFs carry some investment risk because they’re made up of bonds from companies with below-investment-grade credit. However, with additional risk comes the potential for higher returns . Similar to floating-rate CLO ETFs, the coupon rate on senior loan ETFs will increase when the benchmark rate rises.
An example is the State Street Blackstone Senior Loan ETF ( SRLN ). It typically holds 80% of its assets in first-lien senior secured floating-rate bank loans, offering a 30-day SEC yield of 6.78%.
When interest rates rise, equity investors can consider bank stocks because banks’ net interest margin, the difference between interest earned on loans and interest paid to depositors, is also increasing.
“A Fed rate hike boosts banks' net interest margin,” Ebensperger said. “This difference typically increases as the Fed rate rises because banks pass on only a fraction of higher rates to depositors. The positive effect of higher rates on earnings is somewhat mitigated by higher default rates in the face of increased lending rates.”
Investing in bank stocks still carries risk. Even though banks are earning more from mortgages, consumer loans, commercial loans and credit lines, they’re also paying more for deposits, and there can be an increased number of defaults.
If you’re looking to minimize your risk, consider short-term Treasury bills, either held directly or through the iShares SGOV ETF . These have very short maturities, allowing investors to reinvest soon after interest rates rise.

items.title: How is the US-Israeli war on Iran causing havoc in Europe?
items.summary: Rising energy costs and protests are sharpening European opposition to renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
items.content:
Share How is the US-Israeli war on Iran causing havoc in Europe? on social media
Protesters fly a French flag amid clashes in Paris on Saturday [Reuters/Abdul Saboor]
Several Western European nations have expressed their opposition to the potential resumption of the Iran war, as spiralling global oil prices have worsened the cost of living crisis across Europe.
Countries such as Germany and the UK, among other major powers, which initially remained silent on the US-Israeli bombardment of Iran, have aired their views, calling for diplomacy to end the war which has disrupted global oil supplies.

Continued disruption to energy supplies is pushing up household costs as winter in Europe approaches, adding fuel to protests over living standards that have engulfed European capitals in recent weeks.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei on Sunday drew attention to what he described as a shift in Germany’s position on attacks against Iran.
In a post on X, Baghaei recalled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s remarks during Israel’s June 2025 military campaign: “This is the dirty work Israel is doing for all of us.”
He contrasted those words with German officials’ recent warnings against renewed attacks and calls to prevent further escalation, before citing Friedrich Schiller’s The Maid of Orleans, quoting a passage that portrays reason being helplessly dragged towards an abyss by the forces of madness.
Experts say Baghaei’s remarks reflect a broader shift across Europe, where leaders are increasingly questioning their support for the US-Israeli war on Iran.
With Washington reportedly preparing options for renewed attacks, what would further escalation mean for Europe and could the war further strain already frayed relations with the United States?
When the US and Israel launched their attacks on February 28 , the leaders of Britain, France and Germany issued a joint statement condemning Iran’s retaliatory strikes on countries across the region. “We condemn Iranian attacks on countries in the region in the strongest terms,” British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, French President Emmanuel Macron and Merz said.
Their statement did not condemn the opening US-Israeli attacks. However, it called for negotiations to follow. Nearly eight months into the war, European governments are now explicitly warning against another military campaign.
On Friday, the foreign ministers of Britain, France, Germany and Italy met their counterparts from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt in Istanbul to discuss the conflict and the Strait of Hormuz. Further escalation between Iran and the US “would create nothing but losers and would undoubtedly have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.
“And so the first thing this group of eight countries … will do is call on both sides to exercise the utmost restraint, because we cannot afford another escalation in the region,” he added.
The warnings against new attacks do not necessarily mean European governments have abandoned their positions on Iran’s nuclear programme or regional activities, but they do show a change of position and have revealed that European governments are not united in their approach to the Iran war.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has consistently opposed the US-Israeli campaign. At this month’s European summit, he again described the war as “illegal, unjust and unjustified”, linking it to Europe’s mounting economic costs.
Western countries have opposed Iran’s nuclear programme, which Tehran says is for civilian purposes only. European countries were part of the landmark 2015 nuclear deal with Iran that limited Tehran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief. But during his first term in 2018, United States President Donald Trump withdrew from the deal. Both the US and Israel invoked Iran’s nuclear programme to launch their attack in February.
Europe’s divisions have been particularly visible over access to military bases and airspace. “We did not participate in these strikes, but are in close contact with our international partners, including the United States, Israel and partners in the region,” said the February 28 statement from Britain, France and Germany.
But non-participation in the opening attacks did not mean European countries would uniformly refuse support for subsequent operations. Germany said early in the war that it would not restrict US use of its bases, including Ramstein, a major American military hub.
Britain initially withheld permission for the opening attacks. However, it authorised US use of British bases for what London described as specific, limited defensive strikes against Iranian facilities involved in attacks on regional allies. Then, after initial reluctance, Britain expanded that permission to include operations against missile sites and capabilities being used to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
France allowed US support aircraft at Istres, while saying they would support the defence of regional partners rather than participate in attacks on Iran. It later blocked a weapons flight to Israel connected to the campaign. Spain went further. After refusing permission for attacks from the jointly operated Rota and Moron bases, Madrid closed its airspace to US aircraft involved in the war.
Those were different restrictions with different purposes, rather than a single European refusal to cooperate, but they provoked Trump. Calling Spain “terrible”, he threatened to cut off trade and said Washington wanted “nothing to do with Spain”.
The dispute has therefore exposed a widening argument over whether alliance commitments require European governments to facilitate a war they did not choose.
Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera: “As to whether the war might push European leaders to openly challenge Trump, and limit support, it is certainly possible. What was initially a diplomatic disagreement is turning into something that has much more direct … and we could see increased resistance to any support from European countries.”
After Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening strikes, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said there was “renewed hope for the people of Iran”. She also warned then that instability could push the region into a spiral of violence. But by October 16, the costs to Europe had become central to her message. “Households and industry are paying the price for a war far beyond our borders,” she said after an EU summit.
According to von der Leyen, Europe’s bill for imported fossil fuels had increased by 106 billion euros, while gas prices had risen about 140 percent since late February and diesel prices had doubled.
Disruption to Gulf supplies and restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have also caused energy prices to spike. Brent crude settled at $72.48 a barrel on February 27, before the war began. It reached $126.41 at the end of April and remains well above $100 a barrel, with no sign of falling any time soon.
“For Europe, there is the economic interest as well, knowing it would further take a toll on energy markets, pushing up prices at a time when European countries are going into winter and the pushback to that,” Julie Norman, an associate fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera.
Hilborne added that “there is an impact as well on food and fertiliser … The Persian Gulf is a hub for nitrogen-based fertilisers and disruptions have sent prices of urea up by something like 70 percent. Also, supply chains are feeling the impact as well, as shipping companies are facing large increases in their insurance premiums and/or need to reroute to longer journeys”.
“I would say that the Iranian war has had a direct, measurable and quite a rapid impact on European prices,” he added.
The search for relief from the energy crisis has created further friction, with Washington pressing European governments to release emergency diesel stocks, while Trump eased restrictions on Russian diesel in an effort to lower prices. That move provoked criticism from Ukraine and its supporters, who warned that renewed energy revenues would strengthen Moscow’s war effort.
But some of the sharpest political consequences are unfolding closer to home. Protests over living costs, housing, wages and public services have been seen across France, Belgium, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Greece and Albania. Their causes vary, and they do not constitute a single coordinated movement, but experts say the cost of living crisis, compounded by price rises caused by the Iran war, is a common thread that unites the protesters across the continent.
Donatella della Porta, a sociologist and political scientist, told Al Jazeera that opposition to war was central to recent protests by young people across Europe, alongside anger over military spending at the expense of welfare.
She pointed to opposition to military recruitment in schools, weapons-related university research and the use of ports to transport arms, linking those concerns to wider fears about the future.
“Especially the young protesters are afraid that their future will be stolen not only by global warming but also by wars in which they will be sent to die on the battlefield,” she said.
“Young people also connect wars with genocide, having often been socialised into politics during the large protests against the Israeli genocide of the Palestinians.”

items.title: Gaza’s visually and hearing-impaired children miss school due to Israel war
items.summary: Children in Gaza with auditory and visual challenges often have no access to specialist education.
items.content:
Share Gaza’s visually and hearing-impaired children miss school due to Israel war on social media
Kenan al-Sabaa continues his education with great difficulty at a facility designated for students with hearing impairments in the Gaza Strip [Enas Abu Ghayad/Al Jazeera]
Gaza City – With the help of his father, 13-year-old Kenan al-Sabaa attempts to adjust his hearing aid, which has malfunctioned. The plastic tubing and rubber ear mould on the device need fixing, but these parts and the depleted batteries are no longer available due to Israel’s siege on the Gaza Strip.
Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza started in October 2023, Kenan attended the Atfaluna Society for Deaf Children, which provided specialist teaching and opportunities to communicate with other hearing-impaired children.
