But Atfaluna’s building in Gaza City was partially levelled during the war and quickly turned into an overcrowded shelter for displaced people, an example of the widespread destruction of infrastructure in Gaza. This includes the educational institutions disabled children rely upon.
Israeli attacks also forced Kenan’s family to flee to Gaza City’s Jalaa Street. Atfaluna has since set up temporary learning spaces, and Kenan has access to one near where his family now lives. But his father, Tamer al-Sabaa, said the interruptions to his learning during the war have left his son far behind in his studies.
He did not attend school at all during the first year of the war, and now attends classes only for a few hours a week, which Tamer says is not enough given the time he has lost at school during the war.
But Tamer fears that if Israel resumes large-scale attacks – an October 2025 “ceasefire” reduced the number of attacks but did not stop them – he will be forced to stop Kenan from attending.
“These few hours do not cover or repair the massive educational gap and academic decline my son experienced during the war,” Tamer said. “He is in dire need of restoring his equipped educational environment and the specialised care that was stripped away from him.”
“The school operates only three days a week, and for limited hours not exceeding two hours a day,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Being deaf makes Kenan’s movements fraught with danger, as he cannot hear the sounds of explosions, warning signals, or communicate with those around him.”
As a result, Tamer and his wife had to guide Kenan through unfamiliar neighbourhoods to help him learn about his surroundings.
Kenan can now reach school independently, but his safety is always a concern for his parents.
With his father’s help, Kenan al-Sabaa attempts to adjust his hearing aid, which has malfunctioned due to the blockade in Gaza [Enas Abu Ghayad/Al Jazeera] Little help available
The difficulties facing Kenan highlight the effect of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, on disabled children in the enclave.
Fadel Kuraz, a sign language interpreter and disability rights advocate with Atfaluna, said the war has increased hearing-related injuries and severely weakened the services available to children who need support.
“What we are experiencing today in the Gaza Strip represents an unprecedented health and humanitarian setback, and a real catastrophe unlike anything we have seen before,” Kuraz told Al Jazeera.
“To grasp the scale of the tragedy, the baseline number of persons with hearing disabilities registered before October 2023 was around 20,000 people. Today, according to field assessments, approximately 35,000 new individuals … have been added, having suffered total or partial hearing loss due to … explosions.”
Kuraz describes shortages of hearing aids, batteries, ear moulds, and spare parts, alongside major obstacles to specialist hearing tests and treatments. Children also face difficulties accessing visual learning materials because of electricity and communications outages, he said.
“The suffering does not stop at material needs. A deaf child suffers high levels of fear, stress and complex trauma without the ability to verbally express what is on their mind,” Kuraz told Al Jazeera.
Hearing-impaired children in Gaza are more often than not living in overcrowded tents or shelters which lack privacy or a proper space to do homework and study.
“I emphasise that responding to the needs of persons with hearing disabilities is no longer a secondary choice or a luxury; it is an urgent humanitarian necessity,” Kuraz adds. “It requires immediate intervention to break the siege, allow the entry of hearing aids, batteries, and spare parts, and establish safe, temporary alternative educational spaces to replace destroyed centres.”
Children with visual impairments face issues similar to those faced by hearing-impaired children in Gaza, with the few educational facilities once available to them now closed or difficult to access. The materials and items they need to study, such as Braille, are also difficult to procure due to Israel’s siege on Gaza.
Al-Noor school was originally located in Tal al-Hawa, southwest of Gaza City, but was badly damaged in the genocidal war.
Duaa Omar Basheer worked as an educational counsellor at the al-Noor school for blind students in northern Gaza before the war. She said it was the only public school in Gaza designated for middle and high school students with visual impairments, but was forced to close during the war. Some primary education is available to children through educational centres run by the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.
Previously, the school served about 80 pupils from across Gaza, many of whom arrived on dedicated buses, but damaged roads and a lack of suitable transport created further barriers.
Without regular instruction, Basheer fears students could lose their Braille and independent-learning skills, which they have taken years to learn.
“We are facing an entire generation of visually-impaired individuals at risk of illiteracy and academic loss,” Basheer said.
With her mother’s help, visually impaired Jana Shreim studies at home amid a total absence of specialised institutions [Enas Abu Ghayad/Al Jazeera] Broken glasses
In the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City, Jana Shreim’s mother, Wafaa Shreim, says her 12-year-old daughter, who is legally blind, relies on prescription glasses with high magnification and very strong lenses. But she could still only perceive light, shapes and nearby objects.
Her glasses broke amid the harrowing mass exodus from the Shati camp during Israel’s offensive on the neighbourhood in November 2023. The family tried to fix them with wire, but the lenses were damaged beyond use, and replacement glasses were too expensive.
Since the glasses broke – and with no possibility of replacing them due to the blockade – her vision has deteriorated to the point that she can barely see.
Now, when Jana goes to unfamiliar places, she stumbles and falls. Her mother says she is bullied by other children, and that she experiences pain in her eyes when she tries to focus.
“My daughter now has to identify people by their voices,” Wafaa told Al Jazeera. “Her sister and I now act as her ‘eyes’ at every step and everywhere she goes.”
Before the war, Jana attended the al-Noor centre, travelling there on a dedicated bus service. Her school closed when it was badly damaged in Israeli bombing, leaving Jana without any access to education.
“I am currently trying to teach her at home myself using a Braille writing machine we have, so she doesn’t lose her limited educational skills,” Jana’s mother said. She also cares for another daughter with a visual impairment, making it even more difficult to provide the specialist support they both need.
“I searched extensively and knocked on the doors of many institutions and organisations concerned with visual impairment, but the bitter truth is that … we have been left entirely alone,” she said.
“My only message and wish to all responsible parties is to look at our visually impaired children with mercy: provide them with glasses and medical supplies, and open safe educational and recreational spaces that restore their basic right to life and learning.”

Serbia’s strongman Aleksandar Vučić faces the strongest challenge to his 12-year rule in the country, as grassroots protest movement led by Serbia’s students hopes to oust him from office in snap parliamentary elections ( 17:31 ).
The vote comes after nearly two years of widespread protests against alleged government and institutional corruption , triggered by a railway disaster in 2024 ( 17:42 ).
Critics say Vučić, a former information minister of Slobodan Milošević, deploys nationalist playbook in domestic politics, while keeping close ties with Russia and China ( 17:14 ) and not making progress on Serbia’s path towards the European Union ( 17:48 ).
The election takes place amid tense atmosphere with partial turnout data pointing to unprecedented voter mobilisation ( 18:32 , 18:58 ) amid allegations of electoral irregularities with a record-high number of observers following the vote ( 18:00 , 19:11 ).

Meanwhile, there are some first diplomatic reactions to reported incidents at some polling stations across Serbia .
The EU’s ambassador to Serbia Andreas von Beckerath said on X:
“ We are deeply concerned about reported violent incidents across a number of polling stations. Serbian citizens need to be able to exercise their democratic right to vote in a peaceful and safe environment.
We call on all actors to remain calm, to act responsibly and refrain from violence and provocations and on the competent institutions to ensure safety of all involved in the electoral process.”
The US Republican senator Joe Wilson also said on X:
“As the Serbian people take to the polls in historic numbers, I am deeply concerned by reports that the government is potentially preparing to use violence against citizens aimed at obstructing the voting process.
Such attacks are totally unacceptable. I urge Serbia to remain peaceful!”
It was a sunny, if chilly and extremely windy day in London, but none of that seems to have mattered much for the thousands of determined Serbians who turned out to vote at the embassy in Belgravia.
Long queues at the Serbian embassy in central London. Photograph: Jakub Krupa/The Guardian By late lunchtime, the queue stretched hundreds of metres, winding around the elegant blocks of buildings in the embassy district.
Voters near the front reported waiting between two and three hours to cast their vote. Some had travelled from as far afield as Bristol, Cambridge, and Manchester.
Voters wait outside the Serbian embassy in London to cast their ballots in the 2026 Serbian parliamentary election Photograph: Jakub Krupa/The Guardian “Everyone walking to the queue is like, oh, the queue is long , but with a smile on their faces. It’s amazing,” Jovan , 26, said.
Milica , 27, agreed: “I am very happy seeing how many people turned up. I don’t think this was ever the case before.”
“Everyone is happy; for the first time we see people being happy about being in a long queue.”
Both felt today could mark “a start” for something new in Serbia, though Milica voiced concern over how the government might react to the result.
“I am hoping it goes down smoothly tonight [and] there are no conflicts or other incidents. Knowing the government and how things were going during the previous elections, I think there is a chance there might be some trouble today in Serbia, ” she said.
Serbian voters Jovan, 26, and Milica, 27, outside the Serbian embassy in London as they wait to cast their votes in the 2026 Serbian parliamentary election. Photograph: Jakub Krupa/The Guardian Filip , 27, was notably more optimistic: “ I feel freedom in the air. I am really excited. I can’t wait to see the results and hope they will be what I am feeling here [in the queue],” he said.
“I am talking to my family in my home town, my friends in Belgrade, everybody is doing something, is excited. It’s amazing,” he added.
Asked what a potential defeat for Aleksandar Vučić would mean to him, he paused for a moment. “ It means we will finally breathe, ” he said.
“ It feels like we do not have any control or freedom in our own country and people are struggling in every field. It [a possible opposition win] will not fix everything, all of our issues, but it will be an amazing beginning of our future.”
Serbian voter Filip waiting in the queue to vote at the Serbian embassy in London on the day of the 2026 Serbian parliamentary election. Photograph: Jakub Krupa/The Guardian Back to Serbia , a record-high number of over 100,000 people, three times as many as in 2023, registered to vote abroad, but a quirk in the way the overseas vote is organised means that some of them had to cast their votes, erm , at night.
A voter prepares to cast a ballot at a polling station for Serbia’s snap parliamentary elections. Photograph: Sasa Djordjevic/AFP/Getty Images Serbia’s electoral commission has tied voting hours to the local time in Serbia, meaning the voters in the US, Canada or Australia needed additional alarm clocks.
13 polling stations fall victim of this rather unusual arrangement , with voters in Chicago – home to a large Serbian community – forced to vote between 1am and 2pm, and in Sydney between 5pm and 6am. Some of them held impromptu parties as they waited because why not.
The move sparked controversy and accusations of making it difficult for likely opposition voters to cast their ballots, as the tight margins this year suggest that every vote may count.
For example, 28 of the 93 overseas polling stations are in neighbouring Bosnia, where Vučić is particularly popular. In contrast, the US has only four stations, and Canada – two, pushing some voters to make trips of thousands of kilometres to cast their votes.
By the way, Serbia is not the only country hosting elections today or this weekend.
A woman votes during the presidential election, in Sofia, Bulgaria. Photograph: Spasiyana Sergieva/Reuters In the last hour, the polls closed in Bulgaria where voters choose the new president filling the post vacated by populist leader Rumen Radev, who resigned earlier this year to stand in parliamentary elections and take over as prime minister (sort of what Vučić is hoping for).
Moscow-friendly Rumen Radev wins absolute majority in Bulgarian elections
The presidential race pits the acting president and Radev’s former vice-president Iliana Iotova, who would be Bulgaria’s first (elected) female president, against pro-European former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, with a crowded field of 25 other candidates also on the ballot.
Bulgarian president Iliana Iotova delivers a speech during the final campaign rally in Plovdiv, Bulgaria. Photograph: Hristo Vladev/Anadolu/Getty Images Alpha Research’s exit poll from Bulgaria puts Iotova in the pole position after today’s vote, with 35.3% of the vote, just narrowly ahead of Gyurov at 32.4%.
A second exit poll, conducted by Myara research institute, showed similar numbers, with Iotova at 35.2% and Gyurov at 32.2%.
Assuming these numbers are correct, since none of them got the required 50% of the vote, the pair will advance to a runoff next Sunday.
Independent presidential candidate Andrey Gyurov speaks during campaign's closing event in Plovdiv, Bulgaria. Photograph: Valentina Petrova/AP The vote comes at a critical time given the worsening security situation in Ukraine and just days after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships in the Black Sea, including off Bulgaria’s coast.
Intensifying drone attacks on ships in Black Sea bring war ever closer to Nato shores
Somewhat unusually, we will have to rely on vibes a lot this evening (and over the night, as the vote count progress) as … there isn’t much to go by in terms of reliable data on polling intentions.
People wait to vote inside a polling station during the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters Polls are infrequent and show wildly different results, with critics and cynics (you know who you are) saying that they essentially depend on who pays for them or who is the pollster closer to. Whatever the cause, they definitely show all sorts of results.
And so, the final poll done by Ipsos Strategic Marketing (sic!), declared to be paid by Vučić’s list, showed that they are on course for a fairly convincing victory, with 47.4% of the vote, well ahead of the Student List with 40%.
Faktor plus’s polls from September also point to a Vučić win.
But a separate poll by NSPM conducted earlier this month put the Students narrowly – less than 2pp – ahead. To complicate matters further, the Center for Research, Transparency and Accountability’s research from a few months back now gives them an even wider lead, nearing 10pp.
Oh, and to complicate matters further, the polls showed that a not insignificant part of the electorate was still undecided as late as this week.
That’s us trying to figure out what is going on. Photograph: Sasa Djordjevic/AFP/Getty Images We are going to get two projections (note: not exit polls, but based on data from selected polling stations), which are likely to come out around the same time, 9.30/10pm local time (8.30/9pm UK).
That’s the CeSID/Ipsos and CRTA data, based on what they see in their respective samples, as explained in the previous post.
It is not inconceivable that we may end up getting different or outright contradictory suggestions about the result of today’s vote in these projections. Let’s see.
Given we are expecting the result to be fairly close and potentially contested by one or both sides, this all creates perfect conditions for a messy night ahead.
Ultimately, obviously, we will look at the official results, but if they are super close and get contested with recounts, this may take a while.
This will make our work somewhat difficult tonight and will guide us in making cautious calls on the result , but I will try to do my best to guide you through it.
We are essentially getting three different sets of figures tonight: from the electoral commission, from election watchers CeSID and pollster Ipsos, and from another group of election watchers CRTA.
The electoral commission’s data are naturally the most complete, with the latter two groups using their samples – of 750 and 500 polling stations across the country – to report “projected” turnout on that basis.
And to make things easier to follow, they also report at slightly different intervals.
We will need to navigate the three throughout the night, so let me explain this a bit further, using the example of pre-election day polling.
The latest turnout projection by Ipsos/Cesid suggests a turnout of 60.8% by 5pm local time (4pm UK), with three hours still to go until the polling stations close.
That’s more than 13 percentage points higher than in 2023, and would be the highest turnout since mid-2000s.
With three hours to go, it is set to go even higher.
The all-time highest turnout for a Serbian parliamentary election was 71.4%, reported in 1990.
Tired eyes and smiles adorned the faces of thousands of Serbians who woke up early this morning to cast their vote , breaking all turnout records of early voting.
When asked about their motivation to arrive so early at the polling station, Ana, 42, said with a smile:
“ What hasn’t motivated me? There isn’t a single reason I could give that would keep me from showing up at my polling station at 6:20 in the morning.”
Ana, 42, showing the Student List’s three-finger gesture after voting in the 2026 Serbian parliamentary election. Photograph: Ana Milosavljevic/The Guardian Dragana Milić, 60, a member of a polling station committee in the Belgrade municipality of Voždovac, tells us during a cigarette break that she is astounded by the turnout.
“I can’t remember seeing crowds like this at around 8 in the morning in at least the last 15 years.”
Polling station staff Dragana Milić talking to a reporter on the day of the 2026 Serbian parliamentary election. Photograph: Ana Milosavljevic/The Guardian She adds that she’s also surprised by “how polite and well-mannered people have been.” In the weeks leading up to the election, she recounts how various media reports have suggested that there would be significant unrest, which Milić says made her frightened.
A volunteer election observer, Marica , 55, from the IT workers grassroots group “IT in Blockade” also woke up early and arrived at the polling station at 5:15am.
“ The finger ink sprays weren’t working at two polling stations and voting didn’t begin at those polling stations when it was supposed to. More precisely, the ink could be wiped off with wet wipes. Two new sprays arrived, they were tested, and now voting is proceeding without problems, for the time being,” she says.
In Serbia, voters have a finger marked with a special ink only visible under UV light to prevent them from voting more than once.
This is Marica’s first time monitoring an election, a decision which she made because she does not want to allow any kind of electoral manipulation or fraud in this election.
Regarding turnout, she pauses, smiles and says it’s “never been better.”
Volunteer election observer Milica talking to a Guardian reporter on the day of the 2026 Serbian parliamentary election. Photograph: Ana Milosavljevic/The Guardian Since the early morning, we have seen Serbian voters turning out to vote in unprecedented numbers, with projected turnout already at 56.4% by 4pm, just over 14 percentage points higher than at this point in 2023.
Voters queue at a polling station to cast their ballots for Serbia's snap parliamentary elections in Belgrade. Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen
People wait in line to cast their votes during the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/Reuters In fact, it’s already just marginally below the 2023 turnout with another four hours to go, so we are likely to crash some records, way above levels seen in previous years.
Experts seem to believe that this should help the opposition and take it to be the evidence of unprecedented mobilisation following their campaign to get out the vote.
Voters queue at a polling station to cast their ballots for Serbia's snap parliamentary elections in Belgrade. Photograph: Milos Milanovic/AFP/Getty Images Florian Bieber, professor at the University of Graz, told me over the phone from Belgrade, told me that “turnout is really critical in seeing whether they [the students] can potentially succeed tonight.”
But Vučić “is also likely to mobilise voters in different ways than the students do,” he said, so the picture may not be that clear cut.
“There are a couple of unknowns, but overall I would say a higher turnout is overall strongly indicative of a good performance for the students.”
If the result is close – as we are expecting it may very well be – we are likely to hear allegations of voting irregularities and other attempts to influence or outright rig the election process.
A young woman serving as a member of the local electoral committee stands near the door, managing the flow of citizens entering the polling room past an acrylic ballot box in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Aleksandar Jovicic/NurPhoto/Shutterstock After the 2023 election, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights warned that “though technically well-administered”, the electoral process “created unjust conditions” playing to “the ruling party’s systemic advantages”.
It added that “instances of pressure on public sector employees, misuse of public resources, and voter inducement schemes raised concerns about voters’ ability to make a choice free from undue pressure”.
Previous elections have also seen allegations of various forms of rigging, including vote-buying, voter intimidation and ballot box stuffing, which explains an unprecedented number of monitors on Sunday.
There are just over 15,500 domestic observers – three times the 2023 level. The Student List said on Saturday night that it will have representatives in every polling station across the country.
“From the opening of the polling stations to the last vote counted, we will monitor every step of the electoral process. Every ballot, every record, every vote. Every voice has its guardian.”
The Serbian pro-democracy group the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA) said in its interim campaign report before the polling day that there were at least 116 incidents of physical violence and verbal threats against voters, with opposition activites subjected to surveillance, interception and police intimidation.
Its latest update today, it said there were reports of pressure on voters in roughly a third of all polling stations, alongside further procedural irregularities.
CRTA also noted that voters were seen photographing their ballot papers in as many as 40% of polling stations, fuelling concerns that some people might be getting asked to show how they voted.
A growing number of security incidents were also reported on social media throughout the afternoon, including physical intimidation and altercations near polling stations.
We will treat unverified reports of these incidents with caution until the facts are fully established and confirmed.
But CRTA used its latest press conference to urge all actors to reduce tensions and allow the electoral process to run its course.
The country’s public media are also firmly in favour of the incumbent, with “representatives of the authorities” taking 94% of talking time in prime time programmes, CRTA’s report said. The opposition is presented negatively “for more than 80% of the time.”
There are also just over 600 monitors from abroad, including the ODIHR, OSCE, Council of Europe and European parliament’s missions. There are also 31 from Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Georgia ( side eye ).
Acting Serbian president Ana Brnabić accused two MEPs of bias against the ruling party, and questioned their ability to impartially fulfill their duties, according to reports in t he Serbian and Austrian media.
EU foreign spokesperson Christian Wigand responded to her comments on Friday:
“Let me be clear that we take any attempts to discredit members of the European Parliament and the election observers very seriously. Election observation missions deployed by well established international organizations, including by members of the European Parliament are playing an important role to ensure the democratic process and accountability are respected.”
The ODIHR and European parliament delegation will present their preliminary conclusions on the election on Monday afternoon.
Not necessarily that much in substance, but definitely a change in optics.
Unlike most European leaders – with the exception of ousted Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán and his loyal Slovak ally Robert Fico – Vučić has maintained closed ties with Russia, despite the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Last year, he and Fico even controversially joined the Russian Victory Parade in Moscow.
He remains a vocal advocate of “dialogue” with Russia, which he believes to be “a rational, pragmatic” approach to foreign policy. He regularly warns that Europe’s current trajectory makes a third world war “inevitable” and is a stern critic of what he sees as dangerous military buildup across the continent.
Russian president Vladimir Putin and Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic enter the hall during their meeting in Kremlin, Moscow, Russia in May last year. Photograph: Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP POOL/EPA He said in a recent interview with a Russian media personality, Ksenia Sobchak:
“It’s like in Chekhov’s plays: if there’s a rifle hanging on the wall in the first act, that rifle will fire in the third act.”
Vučić has repeatedly rejected any suggestion of imposing sanctions on Russia given the close energy, economic, and trade ties between the two nations. In July, he travelled to Kyiv to take part in a summit of leaders from south-eastern Europe and declined to sign its conclusions calling for support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia.
But hosting Zelenskyy in Belgrade in August, Vučić publicly backed Ukraine’s aspirations to join the EU – despite Serbia’s own process being very much frozen.
Serbian president Aleksandar Vučić and Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy talk during the Carpathian 8 Summit in Bukovel, western Ukraine in September. Photograph: Vladyslav Musiienko/AP Serbia is also believed to have exported hundreds of millions of dollars worth of ammunition to western buyers, which somehow later found its way to Ukraine – despite Belgrade’s repeated denials of any involvement in the war.
Perhaps reflecting the general consensus on the issue - 80% of Serbs opposed sanctions in 2022 , 64% in 2023 – the Student List have also pledged in their manifesto to retain “the traditional partnership” with Russia, and oppose any measures against Moscow.
But … they said in their programme they would “adhere to the international legal position of respecting the territorial integrity” of other countries, including Ukraine, and would “advocate for an end for military conflicts” – whatever that means in practice.
The thorny issue of Serbia’s relationship with Kosovo remains generally highly relevant here. Both Russia and Ukraine do not recognise Kosovo, and Moscow’s strong UN position with its security council veto is particularly helpful in blocking any attempt to challenge the current legal situation.
There is also a practical element: in recent years, Belgrade has also welcomed many Russian entrepreneurs looking for a new base for their headquarters, boosting the local economy.
Serbia has been a candidate country since 2012, with some technical progress made in the last 15 years – but only two “chapters” have been actually closed. The last “milestone” marked on the EU’s website dates to 2021, showing the process has been effectively frozen for the last five years.
EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and Serbian president Aleksandar Vučić hold a joint news conference in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Anadolu /Getty Images The European Commission’s latest rule of law report highlighted several concerns about the country’s justice system, anti-corruption framework, media freedom, and institutional checks and balances. Belgrade also regularly faces criticism over its close ties with Russia and China.
On top of that, in September, the EU strongly condemned the hero’s funeral granted to Ratko Mladić, a Serbian general convicted of orchestrating the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war.
The EU’s enlargement commissioner Marta Kos said “the glorification surrounding [Mladić’s] death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built.”
Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, given hero’s funeral in Serbia
In July, Vučić conceded that Serbia was unlikely to enter the bloc in the coming years.
But if you are expecting the Student List to be unapologetically pro-EU, think again.
Their manifesto on foreign policy includes a very cautiously phrased position on the issue and does not include a clear commitment on the EU membership, primarily stressing the bloc’s importance as Serbia’s “most important economic partner.”
But if you know what to look out for, it does include a pledge to make a technical step in the right direction: the students say they would want Serbia to “achieve IBAR status through significant progress in the area of justice and fundamental rights.”
IBAR – Interim Benchmark Assessment Report – is essentially the European Commission’s finding on whether a country meets accession criteria set out in cluster 1 on fundamentals on democratic institutions, public administration reform, and the rule of law. Montenegro – widely seen as the most advanced candidate country – got there in 2024; Albania – in May 2026.
This sort of vague commitment perhaps makes sense given the List’s much broader focus on deeply reforming the state to get rid of what they see as corruption and systemic injustices. For clerks reading the manifesto in Brussels, it will be enough of a signal to get their hopes up.
Florian Bieber, professor of politics at University of Graz, explained to me as follow:
“ On many divisive issues, like EU integration, there’s no consensus in Serbia.
But you don’t need to do much, because Vučić hasn’t done much.
If the Student List doesn’t do much in a year or two on that issue, but makes Serbia more democratic, it actually achieves a lot more for Serbia and EU integration than what Vučić has done in 10 years, because it’s not about the formal negotiations, but it’s about creating good laws and good functional institutions.”
For what it’s worth, the EU was pretty cautious in its language in the build-up to the vote, stressing that it is “closely following” the election, and insisting it needed to be “free, fair, and transparent” and “in line with European and international standards.”
If the result is very close or contested, many will look out for the EU’s reaction.
The roots of the student movement trace back to the 2024 Novi Sad disaster, where 16 people were killed after an outdoor concrete canopy collapsed at a train station in Serbia’s second largest city.
Rescue service workers inspect a scene as a roof collapsed at a railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia. Photograph: Interior Ministry of Serbia/AP Inquiries into the causes of the incident revealed slipshod construction along with allegations of fraud and corruption, prompting relentless mass protests demanding transparency and accountability about the incident.
‘We are done with corruption’: how the students of Serbia rose up against the system
A protester faces with a Serbia's police officer showing red painted hands symbolising government neglect and mismanagement calls for the resignation of the Minister of Construction in Belgrade. Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen
Students and anti-government demonstrators light the flashlights of their mobile phones during a protest in March 2025. Photograph: Igor Pavicevic/Reuters The demonstrations – primarily organised by students – were frequently met with violence, persecution and extensive surveillance by the authorities, with Vučić repeatedly floating unsubstantiated claims of foreign interference.
When Belgrade students blocked a road in a vigil for the victims three weeks after the disaster, they were attacked by a pro-government mob and the protest movement went nationwide.
Serbian riot police clashes with anti-government protesters in Belgrade in August 2025. Photograph: Marko Djokovic/AFP/Getty Images The student movement eventually morphed into a more political – but not partisan - one.
“Unable to crush the students by force, division or denigration, Vučić gambled, announcing his resignation as president and calling snap elections, in the apparent hope of catching the students off guard, but they responded by improvising a democratic experiment.
The 250 candidates were mostly nominated by university faculties (there are more than 160 doctorates among them) with a sprinkling of farmers and other professions, and each candidate was subject to approval by plenary sessions of the student protests.”
A student protest movement has gripped Serbia for two years. This weekend it will try to take power
In a highly unusual development, however, the group has remained decentralised. For starters, in sharp contrast with Péter Magyar’s Tisza in Hungary, it has no single leader.
A gen Z protest movement could be about to oust Serbia’s strongman. Here’s why that will shake Europe | Misha Glenny
56-year-old cardiologist Ilija Srdanović appears at the top of the ballot, but it is far from obvious if he would be the first pick as a potential future PM.
Instead, the movement focuses on big collective efforts, with large-scale marches across the country and door to door canvassing, including deep in Vučić’s base of rural voters and among typically sidelined minorities.
‘We’ve proved that change is possible’ – but Serbia protesters unsure of next move
It remains to be seen how effective – and disciplined – they would be if they actually succeeded in getting into government. Rewiring the state with all its deeply embedded structural issues after more than a decade of increasingly authoritarian rule would no doubt pose numerous challenges.
As they mount a challenge against Vučić, the students appear to sometimes play on some of the themes of his rule to appeal to his disillusioned voters. Their political manifesto is very carefully constructed to tiptoe around the trickiest issues, particularly in foreign policy, including on Russia and the EU. But eventually they would have to face them head on.
Ivan Đurić of the Center for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA) notes that the students adopted lots of national symbols – including heavy use of flags and the historically-controversial three-finger sign to now denote their number on the electoral ballot – in their rhetoric, but stresses they gave them “a new meaning.”
Supporters of Serbia's student-led movement attend the final campaign rally of the student-backed election list in central Belgrade this week. Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen
Supporters of Serbia's student-led movement attend the final campaign rally of the student-backed election list in central Belgrade. Photograph: Mitar Mitrović/AFP/Getty Images
“Before student movement, if you saw 100 Serbian flags on a protest, you would [think these are] some extreme nationalists, which is also not normal …
But they have shifted the paradigm in this sense … and after years of nationalistic propaganda, it is impossible to expect some kind of extremely liberal, completely pro-European, anti-Russian, peace-making party will get 40%. Not a chance.
But the people who are on this list, … you can imagine them at a table with any partner in the region.”
Marta Szpala of the Polish Academy of Science and BiEPAG research group goes further and contrasts the Serbian model with disruptive and often violent protests movements in western Europe .
“ [The Student List shows] an alternative model: a protest movement that has sustained mobilisation for two years, built a genuine political alternative, and established oversight of its electoral process, standing a chance of bringing about real change.
Serbia may be about to show that achieving change simply requires consistency, perseverance, and the building of broad-based alliances.”
Aleksandar Vučić’s SNS anchors the “United Serbia” list. The party relies on control of the public purse, favourable media coverage and strong nationalist backing, but its campaign has been overshadowed by accusations of systemic voter manipulation.
People walk on a bridge with a huge poster of Serbia's former President and the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) candidate for prime minister Aleksandar Vučić on it, in Niš, Serbia. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters The Student List eschews party hierarchies or a single figurehead, preferring locally respected academics and professionals, and operates through university networks. Its quickfire, humorous campaign has mobilised large numbers of disengaged voters.
Supporters of Serbia's student-led movement attend the final campaign rally of the student-backed election list in central Belgrade. Photograph: Sava Miric/AFP/Getty Images That means Serbia’s traditional opposition parties have been largely marginalised, with their collective support falling from 30% to 10-15%. Some parties have switched allegiance to the Student List. Others, such as European Serbia, may not clear the 3% electoral threshold.
Meanwhile, Serbia’s rightwing, nationalist bloc is riven with disagreements and has been further weakened by the unexpected withdrawal of the We the Power of the People party over allegations of Russian influence. Some of the nationalist vote may switch to the SNS.
What is at stake in Serbia’s election? The key players, main issues and potential fallout
Serbia’s former president and now prime ministerial candidate (again) Aleksandar Vučić rose to prominence in the 1990s as a radical nationalist, who supported the policies of Serbian expansion and ethnic cleansing led by Slobodan Milošević, who died of a heart attack in detention in The Hague during his trial on charges of genocide and crimes against humanity committed in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo.
Serbia's former president and the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) prime ministerial candidate Aleksandar Vučić speaks to the media during the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters He served as Milošević’s information minister throughout the Kosovo conflict. His Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS, has been in government since 2012.
He first spent three years as the prime minister from 2014, before switching to the role of the president in 2017. Unable to run for the third term, he resigned from the post in September, and now wants to lead the government again.
As president, Vučić has not emulated his predecessor’s militarism, but he has maintained his nationalist playbook in domestic politics, dismissing the opposition as stooges of unspecified foreign powers.
He maintains close ties with Putin’s Russia and Xi’s China, which regularly gets him criticism from the EU and complicates Serbia’s path to the bloc.
Russian president Vladimir Putin meets with his Serbian counterpart Aleksandar Vučić in Sochi in November 2021. Photograph: Mikhail Klimentyev/SPUTNIK/AFP/Getty Images Serbia has regressed in international rankings for press freedom and corruption in recent years, and its process of joining the EU is effectively stalled. More on that shortly.
Vučić is also fairly close with Donald Trump and his associates. He hosted Donald Trump Jr and Jared Kushner in Belgrade, and, as we revealed, personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal – and definitely very controversial – scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower.
Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business
Dobro veče , or good evening, and welcome to our live coverage of Serbian election night.
People vote as Serbia holds parliamentary elections in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Andrej Ivanov/Getty Images The grassroots protest movement, the Student List, is taking on the country’s increasingly authoritarian leader, Aleksandar Vučić , in what is shaping up to be the sternest test of his 12-year grip on power.
The vote is a culmination of two years of student-led protests triggered by the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station canopy in November 2024, which killed 16 people and uncovered massive government and institutional corruption.
The bottom-up leaderless movement , with 250 candidates democratically elected from people with limited political experience but distinguished professional careers, seeks to end Vučić’s rule and rewire the state, with focus on fighting alleged corruption, clientelism and power abuses of the past.
Supporters of Serbia’s student-led movement attend the final campaign rally in central Belgrade on Thursday. Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty Images Polls opened at 7am (6am UK time) and close at 8pm (7pm UK time). Until then, we’ll bring you all the key background, explain why it matters for Europe , Ukraine, and you, and give you a flavour of the chatter in the queues outside polling stations from Belgrade to London.
What is at stake in Serbia’s election? The key players, main issues and potential fallout
I will also keep one eye on the first round of the presidential election in Bulgaria , so expect an odd update on this or two on this.
It’s Sunday, 25 October 2026 , it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live .

items.title: Rayner backs Burnham call for debate on return to free movement with EU
items.summary: Cabinet minister says PM’s plea is ‘pragmatism’ but comments risk causing concern among some red wall MPsAndy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers including Angela Rayner but risks causing concern among fellow red wall MPs.The prime minister made his plea for an <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/oct/25/andy-burnham-says-he-wants-honest-discussion-about-freedom-of-movement-with-eu"
items.content:
Angela Rayner and Andy Burham in August. She has said his comments on the EU relationship are ‘just pragmatism’. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Pool AFP/AP
Angela Rayner and Andy Burham in August. She has said his comments on the EU relationship are ‘just pragmatism’. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Pool AFP/AP
Rayner backs Burnham call for debate on return to free movement with EU
Cabinet minister says PM’s plea is ‘pragmatism’ but comments risk causing concern among some red wall MPs
Andy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers including Angela Rayner but risks causing concern among fellow red wall MPs.
The prime minister made his plea for an “honest discussion” about free movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.
Burnham said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].
“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”
His remarks were supported by Rayner, the housing secretary, who told Sky News that it was “just pragmatism”. She said: “It’s about what is the best deal for Britain and that’s what we are asking the public to look at. The prime minister is clear that you can’t take anything off the table when you’re having a conversation.”
Stella Creasy, a Labour MP and the chair of the Labour Movement for Europe, said Burnham was right that the UK was “long overdue for a grownup conversation about what EU freedom of movement actually means to our supply chains and for jobs for British citizens”.
Stella Creasy said the UK was ‘long overdue for a grown-up conversation about what EU freedom of movement means’. Photograph: Milo Chandler/Alamy A number of senior cabinet ministers are keen for the UK to form a much closer relationship with the EU to help boost growth, potentially involving a return to the single market and accepting free movement as a result. Those in favour of reopening the discussion include Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary.
However, Shabana Mahmood , the home secretary, is among those who have been more cautious about the arguments. Mahmood told a New Statesman event at the Labour party conference that rejoining the EU would not be a “simple, straightforward thing” and there were “quite hard trade-offs”, such as eliminating trade friction without “some of the burdens that also brings”.
A number of Labour MPs with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the so-called red wall in the north and Midlands are also wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU. Those include Jonathan Hinder, the MP for Pendle, who recently pressed the prime minister in parliament to rule out a return to free movement.
Concerns were raised on Sunday by Richard Walker, the Labour peer and executive chair of Iceland, who told Times Radio that restarting the debate would be a “dangerous precedent” and that opening the borders would not help the “one million young people that are out of work”.
Burnham’s comments drew an immediate response from the right of politics, with the Conservatives and Reform UK criticising the idea of reopening the debate. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the idea of reopening free movement was “another example of Burnham’s foot-in-mouth syndrome”.
Kemi Badenoch said Burnham ‘hasn’t thought this through or the implications’. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA She posted on social media: “He hasn’t thought this through or the implications. Most people who voted for Brexit did so because they didn’t want free movement. Too many politicians have failed to understand the significance and impact of immigration on communities.
Reform UK plan to target EU nationals based in Britain ‘absolutely outrageous’
“We have had more than enough experience of what happens when politicians, including previous Conservative governments, promise control but fail to deliver it. The answer is to learn from those mistakes, not reopen free movement.”
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, called it a “total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch”. “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty,” he added.
Polling suggests voters in the UK are increasingly open to rejoining the EU or a single market arrangement involving free movement. The concept of free movement was that British and EU citizens could move freely within the bloc, which also shared a single market for goods and services.
During the Brexit referendum, the topic was hotly debated, with the leave campaign arguing that the UK would be able to take control of its borders if it voted to exit the EU. However, in the years that followed, net migration rose to a peak of about 900,000 in January 2020 under a new points-based system, up from 330,000 before the Brexit vote.

Audi’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a rally on Saturday to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia. Photograph: Friso Gentsch/EPA
Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home
VW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVs
Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.
The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia , in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.
The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran , as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.
Volkswagen to cut further 50,000 jobs as it ends row with union over revival plan
Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.
Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.
It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.
Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.
The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories . It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.
Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.
“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”
Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.
However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played a big role in global carbon emissions .

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute are publishing updates Monday through Friday to provide analysis on the war with Iran and the broader Middle East. Weekday updates cover events from the past 24-hour period, whereas weekend updates are abbreviated and cover the Houthi-Saudi conflict and major breaking developments related to the war with Iran.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned on October 23 that US intelligence assessments indicate that Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against US targets in the region.
Houthi supporters and military officers have reportedly expressed dissatisfaction with the group’s military progress near Taiz City and are urging Houthi leadership to conduct a large-scale ground assault to capture the city.
The Houthis claimed that they attacked three Saudi airports, pumping stations on the East-West Pipeline, and oil facilities at major Saudi Red Sea ports.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned on October 23 that US intelligence assessments indicate that Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against US targets in the region. [1] Clayton noted in a memo addressed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Iran has “substantially increased” its efforts to target US personnel.[2] US officials told Western media that US intelligence agencies assess that the Iranian threat to US citizens in the Middle East is at the highest level since the US-Israel-Iran War began in February 2026.[3] Iran has repeatedly targeted US military and diplomatic personnel based in the region since the beginning of the war. Iran also reportedly planned a drone attack against Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford in the United Kingdom, prompting the United States to evacuate 12 B-1 Lancers from the base in early October.[4] US officials told the New York Times on October 23 that the United States has started to reduce its diplomatic personnel in the region due to the threat from Iran.[5]
Clayton’s warning about Iranian plans to attack US targets comes amid recent Iranian threats to “expand” Iran’s target bank in the event that the United States or Israel resume strikes on Iran.[6] Iranian officials warned Arab officials and mediators that Iran would “more aggressively” target US forces and naval vessels in the event of renewed conflict.[7] These warnings are likely intended to deter any renewed US or Israeli military operations while Iran is simultaneously preparing for possible conflict. Iran reportedly conducted over 30 tests of medium-range solid-fuel Emad and Kheibar Shekan ballistic missiles on October 11, for example.[8]
Secure international recognition of Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz
Degrade the US ability and willingness to continue the war
Restore deterrence vis- à -vis the United States and its regional partners
Divide the United States and Israel from the Arab states
Houthi supporters and military officers have reportedly expressed dissatisfaction with the group’s military progress near Taiz City and urged Houthi leadership to conduct a large-scale ground assault to capture the city. The Houthis have fully encircled Taiz City and surrounding areas to the south since October 12.[9] A Marib-based Yemeni journalist and a DC-based Yemen analyst posted social media messages from Houthi-aligned “activists” and military officers who argued that the Houthis’ ongoing siege of Taiz City is providing Yemeni government-aligned forces with excess time to consider options to free the city and exhaust Houthi forces in combat.[10] The messages from the military officers and Houthi supporters claimed that a protracted siege of Taiz City would be a "serious mistake" and bring about “catastrophic consequences” for the Houthis.[11] These messages and reports suggest that some Houthi-aligned figures are not confident in the group’s ability to compel government-aligned forces and civilians to surrender Taiz City, even though government-aligned forces defending the city are engaged in heavy combat and face significant supply shortages.[12]
Yemeni government-aligned forces’ defense of their positions on Taiz City’s western outskirts in recent weeks has also prevented the Houthis from quickly advancing and overwhelming government-aligned forces in the city.[13] Anti-Houthi Yemeni media reported on October 23 that Yemeni government-aligned forces recaptured the Hangar Checkpoint, which lies on a main roadway leading into Taiz City from the southwest, but ISW-CTP cannot verify this claim.[14] Saudi or Yemeni government-aligned forces also conducted at least four airstrikes targeting a major Houthi artillery battery at the abandoned Sofitel Hotel, which is located on a hilltop that overlooks Taiz City from the east.[15] The Houthis have used the hotel’s advantageous terrain to fire heavy artillery barrages on government-aligned forces’ positions in Taiz City since 2015.[16]
Yemeni government-aligned forces are continuing to engage Houthi fighters further south in Taiz and Lahij governorates in attempts to break the Houthis’ encirclement of Taiz City and central Taiz Governorate.[17] Anti-Houthi media posted a video of Yemeni government-aligned forces at a security force headquarters in al Misrakh district, central Taiz Governorate, on October 23 and claimed that government-aligned forces have recaptured the entire district.[18] ISW-CTP cannot confirm this claim, however. An independent Yemeni journalist reported on October 23 that Yemeni government-aligned forces engaged Houthi fighters near the southern edge of the Houthis’ encirclement in Taiz Governorate and along the Taiz-Aden ground line of communication (GLOC) in al Maqatirah district, Lahij Governorate, on October 23.[19] A breakout from the Houthis’ encirclement of central Taiz Governorate will provide little operational gain to Yemeni government-aligned forces unless these forces recapture, hold, and secure significant segments of the Taiz-Aden GLOC.[20]
The Houthis launched at least three ballistic missiles targeting the Yemeni Coast Guard’s administrative buildings in government-controlled Aden on October 24. The Yemeni government’s Interior Ministry confirmed that the Houthis struck a Coast Guard building at its headquarters, located near Aden International Airport, with two ballistic missiles.[21] Houthi military spokesperson Yayha Saree claimed that the Houthis struck the Yemeni government’s al Nasr Military Camp site, where the Yemeni Interior Ministry is now located.[22] The Yemeni government’s Interior Ministry also confirmed that a Houthi ballistic missile struck another Coast Guard building in Tawahi District.[23] Saree claimed that the Houthis also targeted the Naval Base in Aden, which is located in Tawahi District.[24] The Yemeni government’s Coast Guard is responsible for monitoring and intercepting Houthi maritime smuggling efforts.[25] The timing of Houthi strikes targeting government maritime assets is notable given that Saudi Arabia has increasingly struck Houthi smuggling vessels in the Red Sea since October 16.[26]
The Houthis have continued their attack campaign to impose economic and political costs on Saudi Arabia in order to compel Riyadh to capitulate to Houthi demands. The Saudi Joint Forces Command reported that Saudi air defenses intercepted a ballistic missile over Riyadh and a drone over eastern Saudi Arabia on October 23.[27] Saudi air defenses also intercepted ballistic missiles over Yanbu, Taif, Mecca, and Medina on October 24.[28] Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed that the Houthis fired ballistic missiles and drones on October 24 targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Najran International Airport, and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, as well as a Saudi Aramco facility in Yanbu, a Petro Rabigh Refinery in Rabigh, and an unspecified number of pumping stations on the Saudi East-West pipeline.[29] The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi critical infrastructure as part of the Houthis’ ongoing strike campaign to compel Saudi Arabia to halt military operations against the Houthis and accept the Houthis’ demands, which include lifting Saudi controls on Houthi-controlled ports and airports and granting the Houthis control over Yemen’s oil and gas resources.[30]

items.content:
Share ‘Unnecessary’ Iran war, corruption: Takeaways from Obama’s midterm speeches on social media
Obama joins El-Sayed in Michigan rally cry before key midterms
Former President Barack Obama has railed against the Trump administration on a range of issues, including dragging the United States into “an unnecessary war” against Iran, as he campaigned for Democrats in Ohio and Michigan ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Speaking at rallies on Saturday, Obama accused President Donald Trump of “chaos and corruption”, as he urged voters to reject Republicans.
list of 2 items list 1 of 2 Obama joins El-Sayed in Michigan rally cry before key midterms
list 2 of 2 Obama slams Trump’s ‘cruelty and corruption’ as he rallies Democrats
The speeches came just 10 days before the elections, with Senate and gubernatorial races taking place in both states.
Obama blames Trump’s Iran war for rising fuel prices
“The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” Obama said in Cleveland, Ohio, where he rallied in support of former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown.
“Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for,” Obama said.
The former president defended the 2015 nuclear agreement reached under his administration, which restricted Tehran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief.
“Iran didn’t have nuclear weapons because I had put a deal in place that everybody acknowledged kept them from getting nukes, and I didn’t have to fire a missile to do it. I just had to engage in diplomacy,” Obama said.
Obama blamed the conflict for rising oil and diesel prices, citing attacks on US military bases, American casualties and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
“Our allies and our bases have been attacked. Americans have been killed, hundreds of Americans have been wounded. We have run down our stock of missiles, and Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz where oil goes through to the world market,” he said.
The disruptions in oil flow through the strait, located between Iran and Oman, have pushed up energy prices worldwide. Before the war, a fifth of global oil and gas passed through the strait, which Iran has used as leverage in the war.
“This is the reason why the price of oil is up … This is the reason the price of diesel is up.”
The spike in diesel and petrol prices will likely cost the Republican Party, as the majority of Americans hold Trump responsible for starting the war and the subsequent increase in prices.
Obama also mocked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his focus on military culture and the Pentagon’s plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.
Tariffs are making life more expensive for Americans
Obama criticised Trump’s tariffs, saying Americans were paying more for goods, including products made in the US using imported parts.
“When you impose tariffs, consumers pay the tab,” he said.
“It’s not just the goods that you use directly that have been imported … It’s also the car you build here in America. They might need a part from somewhere else, and now suddenly there’s a tariff on it.”
He questioned Trump’s trade dispute with Canada, a major US trading partner.
The two countries have been locked in a trade dispute, with Trump threatening 50 percent tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts from January 2027.
“And the big trade war he’s starting now is with that well-known evil empire Canada,” Obama said sarcastically.
“Canadians are the nicest people … they’re like our friendly neighbours to the north, and he’s like picking a fight with them.”
Obama also pointed to the growing US national debt, which has reached $40 trillion.
“Instead of bringing down deficits like he said with these tariffs, we’re now running a debt to the tune of $40 trillion.”
The figure refers to the total federal debt, which has accumulated over successive administrations, rather than the annual budget deficit.
Obama accused the Trump administration of favouring wealthy Americans while common households struggled with rising costs.
“After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough,'” Obama declared. “We are voting for change right here in Ohio.”
He pointed to Trump’s 2025 tax and spending legislation, which extended tax cuts while reducing federal spending on programmes including Medicaid and food assistance.
“The only bill they passed of any significance in the last two years was a trillion-dollar tax break that mostly benefitted the richest Americans,” he said.
Obama also took aim at Trump’s White House renovations, including plans for a ballroom, changes to the Rose Garden and the addition of gold decorations.
“He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama joked.
“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory, just gold everywhere.”
The former president said the US needed secure borders but criticised the methods used by immigration agents under the Trump administration.
“I believe that we do need to make sure that our border is orderly and secure and that people who want to come here do so lawfully,” he said.
“But I don’t recall anybody campaigning on sending masked agents running through our streets. I don’t recall anybody talking about law-abiding citizens being arrested, detained, or shot.”
“That’s not what we have to do to get our borders under control,” he added.
Obama attacks Ramaswamy over controversial Amy Acton advertisement
In Ohio, Obama criticised Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy over a campaign advertisement featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.
The advertisement features Acton’s mother questioning her honesty and her account of her childhood, without mentioning the allegations of sexual abuse that led to their separation decades ago.
It has drawn criticism from Republicans, including Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, although Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended it.
Obama condemned Ramaswamy’s decision to use Acton’s family history in the campaign.
“There’s got to be something inside you where you just say, you know, no office is worth stooping that low,” he said.
He also praised Acton’s career in public service and urged Ohio voters to support her on November 3.
Obama urges Michigan voters to back El-Sayed and Benson
In Detroit, Obama campaigned for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and gubernatorial contender Jocelyn Benson.
He praised El-Sayed’s Michigan roots and criticised his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, over his support for the US-Israel war on Iran and Trump’s trade policies.
“Abdul is as Michigan as it gets,” Obama said, referring to his upbringing in the state, his family’s ties to the auto industry and his involvement in school sports.
Obama also spoke about attacks on El-Sayed’s Muslim identity, comparing them with false claims about his own religion and birthplace during his presidential campaigns.
“Unlike Mike Rogers, Abdul hasn’t spent months cheerleading the Iran war … or called these tariffs ‘masterful’.”
The former president pushed back against those who call El-Sayed a “radical”, declaring that “Abdul shares my values”.
Obama also praised Benson for standing by Michigan’s 2020 election results despite threats and protests outside her home.
“When armed protesters showed up outside her home in 2020, demanded she overturn Michigan’s fair and free election results, Jocelyn stood her ground, stood up for you and your rights,” he said.
Obama calls midterms a ‘circuit breaker’ against Trump
Obama said the midterm elections offered voters a chance to limit Trump’s power during the remaining two years of his presidency.
“This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration,” he said. “It’s the circuit breaker in the system. We need to flip that circuit breaker.”
He also warned that dishonesty, intimidation and bullying were becoming accepted in US politics.
“We are not going to fix the economic system or the political system … so long as we’ve got a culture where anything goes and where people in the highest offices in the land think it’s OK to lie and cheat and bully,” he said.
“What we are missing in our public discourse is just basic decency.”

items.content:
After years of record-breaking growth, major market indexes have stagnated. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.52% ) and the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI -1.23% ) have each dipped by around 2% from their all-time highs, while the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -0.21% ) has slipped by close to 6%.
Investors are also feeling conflicted about the future of the market. Nearly 46% of investors believe stock prices will fall over the next six months, according to the latest weekly survey from the American Association of Individual Investors, while 37% are bullish about the future, and the remaining 17% expect little change.
While it's impossible to predict how stocks will perform in the coming months, the market is sending a warning signal that has only been seen during the dot-com bubble. Here's how investors can prepare right now.
In the late 1990s, tech stocks were booming as excitement about the internet reached fever pitch. Many tech companies saw record-breaking initial public offerings (IPOs), reaching valuations that were astronomical for the time. Between 1995 and 1999 alone, the S&P 500 soared by close to 200%.
Another metric that was reaching record highs, though, was the S&P 500 Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio. This ratio measures the S&P 500's long-term valuation, with higher figures suggesting that the index is overvalued.
Historically, higher ratios have been followed by a drop in stock prices, and this metric has predicted market crashes such as the 1929 Great Depression. In early 1999, the ratio surpassed 40 for the first time in history as the dot-com bubble grew. Just over a year later, in March 2000, the bear market officially began.
Now the CAPE ratio is elevated again. The metric surpassed 40 in May of this year, where it's remained ever since. This is only the second time in history that it's stayed this high for months at a time.
To be clear, this doesn't necessarily mean we're headed toward a dot-com-style crash. This metric provides a snapshot of the market's valuation over time, but it can't predict when the next bear market will begin, how severe it might be, or how long it might last.
That said, it does suggest that stocks are incredibly richly valued, making this the priciest market in decades.
If a recession or stock market crash is coming, the best move investors can make is to buy quality stocks and hold them for the long term.
Companies with weak foundations will have a harder time rebounding from downturns, and some may not recover at all. Countless tech stocks soared to record valuations in the 1990s, for example, only to go bankrupt just a few years later when the bubble popped. The tech stocks that survived were those with healthy finances, a durable competitive advantage, and capable leadership teams.
Even healthy companies can experience severe short-term volatility, which is why a long-term outlook is key. Microsoft , for example, plunged by 60% during the dot-com bear market. Apple lost more than 51% of its value in a single trading day in 2000. And Amazon sank by a staggering 94% between 1999 and 2001.
Now, all of these stocks are industry-leading giants, and the investors who reaped the greatest rewards were those who held on and continued investing even during the bleakest moments.
No two bear markets are identical, but even if history is repeating itself and we're staring down another market crash, the smartest investors aren't panicking. Rather, they're loading up on healthy stocks with robust fundamentals , and they're giving those investments plenty of time to generate life-changing wealth.
In the wise words of Warren Buffett: "Keep buying it through thick and thin, and especially through thin."

Saudi Arabia’s coalition said it intercepted Houthi drones and missiles aimed at Riyadh, Khamis Mushait and the southern region.
The Houthis said they targeted airports and energy sites, including King Khalid International Airport and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu.
Rising tensions and concerns about possible fresh U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran helped push Brent crude to a six-month high Friday.
The U.S. embassy HQ in Riyadh is pictured on March 3, 2026.
Saudi Arabia intercepted drones and missiles headed for several cities, including the capital Riyadh, fired by Iran -aligned Houthis on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said.
The ongoing fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Yemen-based Houthis, combined with remarks by President Donald Trump last week suggesting that the U.S. and Israel are planning fresh strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, drove oil prices to a six-month high Friday.
The official Saudi Press Agency quoted the spokesperson of the Saudi-led Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen, Turki Al-Maliki, as saying two drones and a ballistic missile were "intercepted and destroyed" as they headed toward Riyadh.
The agency quoted Al-Maliki as saying that 10 ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward the southern region of Saudi Arabia were also intercepted, as was a cruise missile headed for the city of Khamis Mushait.
The Houthis said in a Telegram post that they "carried out seven qualitative military operations using a number of ballistic missiles and drones."
The targets included Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and oil giant Saudi Aramco's facilities in Yanbu on Saudi Arabia's west coast as well as other airports and energy installations around the country, the Houthis said.
Smoke and flames rise from King Khalid Airport, after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis said they attacked the airport, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 8, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video.
King Khalid International Airport said in a notice to travelers that it was resuming operations Sunday, using its Terminal 1 for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for overseas routes.
The airport suspended operations on Oct. 10 following a strike that killed at least 13 people and injured around 300 others, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Saudi Aramco did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Resumption of Iran attacks 'fairly soon'?
While the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have been exchanging strikes in recent weeks, concerns have been mounting among investors that the U.S. could soon resume its attacks on Iran.
The U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia last week amid the Houthi attacks.
Trump said Wednesday that the U.S. was not negotiating with Iran and something would happen "fairly soon."
The president's cryptic remarks came as U.S. officials told The New York Times that the U.S. and Israel have plans for fresh strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.
Sen: Middle East escalation is a matter of ‘when’, not ‘if'
"I think there's more and more fears of escalation in the Middle East," Amrita Sen, Founder and Director of Energy Aspects, told CNBC's Squawk Box Europe on Friday.
"We keep getting asked by clients: 'Is it going to be before the midterms? Is it after the midterms?' So it's not a question of 'if.' People are asking if it's a question of 'when.' Our view remains that it's more likely after the midterms than before."
Rising tensions, worries about supply disruptions and concerns about possible fresh U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran helped push Brent crude to a six-month high Friday.
Brent futures gained 3.1% to close at $116.72 a barrel, the highest international benchmark settlement since April 29. U.S. West Texas Intermediate added 3.8% to settle at $103.27 a barrel. Brent added 6.2% for the week, the third consecutive week of gains. WTI advanced 2.3% for the week.

items.content:
Libya Opens Al-Rashad Gas Field, Restarts Brega Refinery | Egypt Oil & Gas
Libya Opens Al-Rashad Gas Field, Restarts Brega Refinery
Libya’s National Oil Corporation (NOC) has brought the Al-Rashad gas field online with a production capacity of 50 mmcf/d and restarted the Brega refinery and a natural gas processing unit after prolonged shutdowns, the corporation said on October 25.
NOC Chairman Masoud Suleiman announced the opening of the gas field south of Brega to mark the 65th anniversary of the first oil shipment exported from Brega port in 1961.
The field’s production capacity is 50 mmcf/d, and its output is expected to support natural gas supplies for power plants and industrial users.
The NOC also announced the restart of the Brega refinery, operated by Sirte Oil Company, following a major maintenance overhaul.
The work included replacing the catalyst, upgrading control systems, and installing a new control room.
Separately, Sirte Oil Company restarted the natural gas processing unit at the Brega complex after years offline. The unit will process 60 mmcf/d of natural gas for delivery to the gas network instead of flaring, helping reduce emissions and improve resource utilization, the NOC said.
